papers.title: Multi-source Data Analysis for Assessing Active Slow-moving Landslides Exhibiting Limited Geomorphic Evidence: the Santa Cecilia Case Study (Northern Apennines, Italy)
papers.summary: The detection and kinematic assessment of slow-moving landslides in geologically complex settings can be challenging, especially when the landslides exhibit limited geomorphic evidence despite being active. The Santa Cecilia landslide, located in the Piacenza Apennines (Northern Italy) is one of these cases. This study aims to a preliminary characterization of the landslide through the integrated analysis of geomorphological observations, subsurface investigations, and multi-temporal monitoring data. High-resolution UAV-LiDAR (Unmanned Aerial Vehicle) data were used to support geomorphological mapping and the identification of surface features. Subsurface conditions were investigated through geophysical investigations, boreholes, and inclinometer monitoring, providing constraints on lithological heterogeneity and deformation depth. Multi-Temporal Synthetic Aperture Radar Interferometry (MT-InSAR) analysis, based on Sentinel-1 data acquired between 2019 and 2024, was applied to detect and quantify surface displacements, from both ascending and descending orbits, allowing assessment of the influence of satellite line-of-sight geometry on displacement detection. The integration of MT-InSAR results with inclinometric measurements highlights spatial variability in deformation rates within the landslide body, with more active sectors showing coherent kinematic signals across independent datasets. Results suggest a transition from brittle deformation affecting competent lithologies in the upper slope to more distributed movement within fine-grained materials downslope. Although the proposed kinematic model is preliminary, it provides a coherent framework for interpreting landslide dynamics and for guiding future monitoring and investigation campaigns, aimed at defining the most appropriate rick mitigation strategies.

papers.title: Landslide Hazard Mapping in Tbilisi (Georgia)
papers.summary: Geological hazards such as landslides, debris ﬂows, rock avalanches, rockfalls has always been and still represents a major threat for communities all over the world, causing extensive damage and often times the destruction of infrastructures and facilities. Geological-related, adverse phenomena are more frequent in mountainous countries with complicated geological, tectonic, climate and morphological settings. Tbilisi has a very convenient location and is not only the capital of the country, but also a hub of the transit corridor. However, in the conditions of complex morphological and geological environment, as well as high pressure of technogenic activities, geo-ecological complications have reached a critical level. Within the framework of a program led by Department of Geology of Georgia, landslide hazard assessment was done. Based on the analysis and generalization of produced (historical) materials, laboratory and field studies, the research evaluates the combination of factors that determine the tendencies of landslide hazards. Landslide processes are widespread, causing economic loss and damage to the city's infrastructure and, most tragically, often resulting in human casualties. Surveys in the study area revealed different type of landslides, based on that inventory map and GIS database was created/updated. Geological maps published in the last century were revised and updated, as well as various thematic (elevation, slope and aspect) maps were processed. Based on all this information, a hazard zoning map was compiled. Research classifies the protective adaptation measures, which are necessary to mitigate or completely eliminate the hazards, according to their type and genesis.

papers.title: Landslide Mitigation in Volumetric-Sensitive Soils: Integrated Stabilization Design for the Kalibeng Formation
papers.summary: Landslides and ground movements significantly threaten Semarang City, Indonesia, particularly in the Deliksari area. This region’s vulnerability stems from its location within the Kalibeng Formation, characterized by brownish-gray marly clay identified as montmorillonite. This expansive clay, combined with complex geological structures like joints and faults, creates high soil porosity and erosivity, leading to discontinuous layers prone to failure. This study conducts a geotechnical assessment and stability analysis. Field investigations via cone penetration tests (qc) yielded a cone resistance of 82 kg/cm² (8.04 MPa) at 20 m depth. Laboratory results showed a Liquid Limit (LL) of 148.12% and free swell of 425%. Using the Stark and Eid correlation, we determined the average friction angle (ϕAverage) to be 12.65°. Back-calculation via GeoStudio on the existing slope revealed a critical Safety Factor (SF) of 0.343. To mitigate instability, we modelled two reinforcement simulations. The first, utilizing a counterweight, gabions, bamboo piles, and one 600 mm diameter bore pile, yielded an SF of 0.684. The second simulation, which added a second bore pile, significantly increased stability to an SF of 1.611. Consequently, the recommended design features a 1V:5H slope counterweight supported by two bore piles, gabions, and 4 m deep bamboo piles. To manage pore water pressure, a 60 cm sand drain wrapped in non-woven geotextile is integrated between the embankment and original soil.

papers.title: LiDAR for Rapid Geomorphological Assessment, Examples in Relict Periglacial and Landslide Landsystems
papers.summary: Areas of relict periglacial (permafrost) landforms, including landslides, cambering, valley bulge and associated gulls are often challenging to delineate from ground mapping alone. This submission presents the advances in ground model assessment offered by airborne LiDAR (laser scanning) data sets for engineering geomorphology. High resolution digital elevation models derived from the LiDAR imagery can be utilized to interpret and visualize the on-ground geomorphology. The available LiDAR imagery is described, and examples of their use presented from classic case study sites.

papers.title: Influence of hydraulic conductivity variability on slope stability modelling in a first-order watershed
papers.summary: Abstract In landslide studies, the definition of geotechnical and hydrological parameters provides the basis for deterministic slope-stability modelling. However, their availability and spatial representativeness remain important limitations for watershed-scale applications. This study evaluated the influence of different saturated hydraulic conductivity (K sat ) spatialization approaches on Factor of Safety (FS) estimates using a deterministic slope-stability model in a first-order watershed. A Digital Terrain Model was used to derive morphometric and hydrological parameters, while field measurements of K sat supported three parameterization approaches: morphology-based, inverse distance weighting (IDW), and a single representative value. Instability scenarios were evaluated using a landslide scar inventory, and soil samples from six K sat measurement points were used to characterize particle-size distribution. Among the tested parameter configurations, maximum soil depth and initial groundwater-table depth produced greater differences in model results than K sat spatialization. K sat showed limited spatial variability, with measurements at 30 cm depth spanning from 10⁻³ to 10⁻⁵ m s⁻¹, whereas those at 50 cm were concentrated around 10⁻⁵ m s⁻¹. Higher clay contents with depth at some sampling points may have contributed to the observed decrease in K sat . Overall, within the observed range of K sat variability, a single representative value provided a practical alternative to spatially distributed parameterization in the studied first-order watershed. These findings are applicable to first-order watersheds where shallow landsliding is recurrent; broader applications involving greater geomorphological diversity and different predominant slope processes may require K sat characterization across a wider range of geomorphological compartments.

papers.title: Slowing a Large Landslide to Maintain a Highway
papers.summary: In August 2023, cracking across both lanes of State Highway 1 (‘SH1’) was observed near Utiku, New Zealand. The locations of the mapped cracks coincided with the headscarp of the existing Utiku Landslide, a large, deep-seated, slow-moving landslide that has intermittently impacted SH1 and the North Island Main Trunk railway, since at least the 1960s. The surface cracking and deformation resulted from renewed movement of the landslide along the basal failure plane some 55-75 m below SH1, caused by elevated groundwater levels resulting from many months of above-average rainfall. A remedial design involving four components was developed: (i) minor road realignment, as well as undercut and subgrade improvement; (ii) installation of fanned inclined drains to relieve groundwater pressure and improve landslide stability; (iii) surface water and pavement drainage improvements; (iv) ongoing instrumentation and monitoring. The fanned inclined drains almost immediately had significant impacts on groundwater levels, in places lowering them by close to 9 m. This paper addresses the geology and history of the Utiku Landslide, and how this informed the remedial design. The assessment of the 2023 landslide movement, the design of the fanned inclined drains, including the performance-based approach to optimising design and construction, as well as the monitoring results which show the beneficial impacts of the drains on groundwater levels and landslide stability are discussed in detail. We conclude by providing recommendations for the application of this approach to similar projects.

papers.title: Impact of clustered landslides on strategic road network in central Italy during a rapid snow–rainfall sequence
papers.summary: No abstract available

papers.title: Monitoring of Subsoil Deformations for a More Correct and Complete Interpretation of Slow or Extremely Slow Kinematic Phenomena
papers.summary: Technological improvements have led to a significant increase in the use of remote sensing and proximal remote sensing techniques in the field of landslide monitoring in the last decade. These systems enable the characterization of unstable area evolution at various scales and sample rates. Particular interest is in phenomena characterized by slow or very slow kinematics, which, over time, can induce medium- and long-term stress and critical issues, especially on large infrastructures (railway and road lines, dams, etc.). In this context, it is crucial to observe deformation dynamics both on the surface and underground. Surface observation alone can sometimes hide (or mask) the true and complex deformation dynamics occurring underground. Deformation measurements must therefore also be performed on the subsoil with a correct temporal frequency, adequate vertical discretization, but also with sustainable long-term costs. We present results from extremely deep inclinometer monitoring activities (up to approximately 250 m), conducted using robotic inclinometer systems with almost daily measurement frequencies. The system used, equipped with a single biaxial probe operated by a robotic system, allowed for the acquisition of high-quality measurements useful for a more complete and correct interpretation of process kinematics (both above and below ground). The results obtained with a 50 cm discretization and double reading (0/180°) confirm that it is possible to obtain high-quality measurements in even complex contexts, but also that the data must be analyzed appropriately.

papers.title: A Comparative Slope Stability Analysis Using Empirical Methods in Kumaun Himalaya, Uttarakhand, India
papers.summary: The Himalayas are prone to natural hazards such as cloudbursts, landslides, flash floods, and earthquakes. The engineered/natural slopes along the national highway (NH)-109, from Jaurasi to Chausali in the Lesser Kumaun Himalayas, are significantly influenced by tectonic activity, lithologic diversity and external factors such as precipitation and seismic triggers. Construction and road expansion along highways pose major protection concerns in mountainous regions. Slope stability assessment requires a thorough understanding of the mechanical behaviour of rock masses, including structural deformation and intact rock geo-mechanical parameters. This study assessed two vulnerable road-cut slopes in Nainital and Almora districts, Uttarakhand, India, using empirical classification systems. Field data on slope geometry and discontinuity sets, along with laboratory data on intact rock characteristics, were collected. These datasets were used for kinematic analysis and empirical rock mass classification methods, such as the basic rock mass rating (RMRb), continuous slope mass rating (CSMR), and slope mass rating (SMR). On the basis of comparative assessment of the aforementioned classification systems, both slopes showed instability, and remedial measures such as rock bolting with wire mesh and a toe wall/ditch, and shotcrete with surface drainage are required to mitigate landslide incidents. This multifaceted study will help mitigate landslide vulnerability along this corridor and improve safety for commuters.

papers.title: Assessing the Feasibility of Crowdsourced Pavement Roughness as a Proxy for Landslide Impacts on Roads in Italy
papers.summary: Monitoring landslide impacts on transport infrastructure remains challenging at national scale, where systematic damage surveys and high-resolution monitoring are rarely feasible. This study explores the potential of using crowdsourced road pavement roughness data as a proxy indicator of landslide-related road degradation across Italy, with particular emphasis on the contrast between national- and regional-scale analyses under heterogeneous data conditions. Vehicle-based pavement roughness observations from the SmartRoadSense platform were spatially intersected with the Italian Landslide Inventory (IFFI) and analyzed at both national and regional scales. Pavement roughness distributions inside and outside mapped landslide polygons were compared using descriptive statistics and nonparametric approaches. Results show that at national scale, median pavement roughness values inside and outside landslide areas are comparable, with substantial overlap between distributions, limiting the interpretability of roughness as a uniform proxy. In contrast, regional-scale analyses reveal highly variable behaviour: several regions exhibit higher roughness within landslides, others show weak contrasts, and in some cases higher roughness occurs outside mapped landslides. These differences reflect regional variability in landslide inventory completeness, roughness data coverage, and spatial correspondence between mapped landslides and deformation zones. These findings highlight both the potential and the limitations of crowdsourced pavement roughness for large-scale screening of landslide–road interactions. While national-scale aggregation tends to obscure landslide-related signals, regional analyses provide more informative results where data conditions are favourable. This emphasises the need for scale-aware interpretation when integrating crowdsourced infrastructure proxies into landslide risk frameworks, particularly for early-warning applications.

papers.title: Risk Assessment of Bridges Affected by Landslides
papers.summary: Following the collapse of the Morandi Bridge in 2018, the Italian National Guidelines introduced a multi-level procedure for the classification, safety assessment, and monitoring of existing bridges, identifying landslide risk as one of the main risks (along with structural seismic and hydraulic risks) affecting the safety of the infrastructure. Within this framework, the MARIE project (Methodological Approaches for RIsk assessment in the framework of landslide-bridge IntEraction), promoted within the Consorzio FABRE, aims to improve and standardise the operational assessment of bridge-landslide interaction, with particular reference to Special Inspections and Level 4 detailed assessments. The project addresses the main uncertainties that emerged during the application of the Guidelines, including incomplete inventory data, poorly constrained landslide geometry and kinematics, suspected or non-inventoried phenomena, and the definition of appropriate investigation and monitoring strategies. Preliminary results highlight the need to place preliminary geological and geotechnical models at the core of the assessment process, as a link between risk classification and accurate safety verification. These models support the identification of interaction scenarios, the optimisation of investigation campaigns, and the integration of monitoring data, remote sensing and physically based analyses for rainfall-induced processes. The proposed methodology provides a more coherent and reproducible pathway for landslide risk management of existing bridges. It contributes to reducing decision-making uncertainty, supporting future refinements of the Guidelines and improving the safety, resilience and durability of critical infrastructure exposed to evolving geomorphological and climatic conditions.

papers.title: Assessing the Added Value of InSAR Deformation Features for Landslide Susceptibility Mapping Using Spatial Validation and SHAP
papers.summary: Conventional landslide susceptibility assessments rely primarily on static environmental factors, which provide limited information on actual slope movement. The additional predictive value of interferometric synthetic aperture radar (InSAR) deformation features, and the consistency of this value, remain insufficiently established. This study assessed their contribution to landslide susceptibility mapping in Luding County, Sichuan Province, China. Sixteen static environmental factors were combined with three features derived from small baseline subset InSAR (SBAS-InSAR): long-term mean deformation velocity (Vmean), velocity variability (Vstd), and velocity trend (Kv). Random forest (RF), XGBoost (XGB), LightGBM (LGBM), and CatBoost (CAT) models were evaluated using 30 repeated spatial holdout splits and paired ablation experiments. Adding Vmean yielded modest median paired AUC gains of 0.003–0.005 across the four models under the primary 10 km spatial validation scheme. XGB achieved the highest mean AUC (0.914) with the M1 feature set, comprising the static factors and Vmean. Adding Kv or Vstd did not yield consistent further gains. Out-of-sample Shapley additive explanations (OOS-SHAP) identified rainfall, the coefficient of variation in elevation (CV), distance to faults, and lithology as the leading predictors; Vmean also made an appreciable contribution. The main predictors exhibited nonlinear responses. Spatial SHAP mapping and Moran’s I analysis further revealed pronounced spatial variation and significant clustering in feature contributions. These findings indicate that long-term mean InSAR deformation velocity provides a consistent but modest complement to conventional static factors, primarily through local adjustments to predicted susceptibility and the identification of regional differences.

papers.title: Reimagining Landslide Early Warning Systems in the Global South: A Systematic Review of Thresholds, Hydro-Mechanical, and Predictive Architectures
papers.summary: A structured matrix was used to extract the trigger, model, and threshold type; model output; bibliographic information; rainfall data source; warning-system features; reported performance; limitations; and recommendations. Studies were further categorized into model types (empirical, physically based, machine learning, probabilistic, and hydro-mechanical models).

papers.title: Numerical Modeling of Tunnel Deformation near the Panagopoula Landslide in Greece using Finite Element Methods
papers.summary: This study focuses on the analysis of ground deformations during the excavation of the south branch of the twin tunnel T26, constructed adjacent to the Panagopoula landslide — one of the largest landslides recorded in Greece. The tunnel, part of the Elefsina–Korinthos–Patras motorway, crosses a geologically heterogeneous zone dominated by limestones, cherts and Pleistocene conglomerates belonging to the Olonos-Pindos nappe system and affected by the active extensional tectonics of the Gulf of Corinth region (Central Hellenic Shear Zone). Ten geotechnical units (GU) were defined along the alignment, of which seven were encountered in the south bore that is analysed in this study. A combined analytical–numerical framework is applied: preliminary elastoplastic analysis using the convergence-confinement method provides stress-release coefficients, which are then used as staged-excavation inputs for two-dimensional finite element models based on the generalised Hoek-Brown failure criterion. The influence of the landslide on tunnel behaviour is manifested through degraded rock-mass quality, characterized by a low Geological Strength Index (GSI), rather than through direct modification of the in-situ stress regime, a distinction that is explicitly addressed in the methodology. Results show that crown displacements range from approximately 8 mm in competent limestones (GU-II(L), GSI 50) to 88 mm in poorly cemented conglomerates (GU-II(c), GSI 30), with the most critical sections requiring closed-type invert support. The combined approach is validated by internal consistency between analytical and numerical predictions, and its non-circular character is demonstrated.

papers.title: Erosion Mechanisms of Landslides: Granular Column Collapse Experiment on Erodible Beds and DEM Insights
papers.summary: Dynamic erosion and entrainment of loose path materials can fundamentally reshape the mobility, kinematic stages, and deposition morphology of rapid granular landslides. However, it remains challenging to isolate controlling factors because erosion results from coupled momentum transfer, bed deformation, and local mass exchange at the particle scale. This paper investigates erosion development during granular column collapse over erodible beds through laboratory experiments and three-dimensional discrete element method (DEM) simulations. A transparent flume (120 cm long, 80 cm high, 20 cm wide) was used to release granular columns onto a 5 cm-thick erodible layer, enabling systematic comparisons across material combinations and initial aspect ratios while minimizing wall effects by ensuring a sufficiently large flume-width-to-particle-size ratio. Experiments were repeated three times for each condition to ensure reproducibility. Three distinct regimes were identified from synchronized observations of free-surface evolution, erosion-interface migration, and front kinematics: (i) non-erosion, (ii) overriding (covering) erosion, and (iii) plunging (penetrating) erosion. Front-position evolution exhibits a characteristic S-shaped trajectory with acceleration, quasi-steady propagation, and deceleration stages. Erosion significantly prolongs the initial acceleration and final deceleration stages while shortening the quasi-steady stage, yet the total flow duration remains proportional to the free-fall timescale. DEM results reproduce these trends and reveal that the particle density ratio between the column and bed governs regime transitions, whereas particle size ratio and initial aspect ratio play secondary roles.

papers.title: Slope Geohazard Susceptibility Zonation Along a Mountainous Highway: A Case Study of the Sichuan-Tibet Highway, China
papers.summary: The Sichuan-Tibet Highway is considered the link between Tibet and eastern China, which is of strategic importance to China. The frequent occurrence of collapses/rockfalls and landslides in this region has attracted wide attention from geoengineering scholars. Various kinds of evaluation methods were employed for the susceptibility of geological hazards. Based on the analysis of the geological environment, seven main factors correlated with the development of slope geohazard were obtained, including lithology, tectonics, aspect, slope gradient, elevation, river system, and land use type. The susceptibility of slope geohazard in the region was predicted using the certainty factor method. The evaluation results were validated using the area under the curve method. The study area was divided into 5 levels based on the combination of the assessment results and field investigation. Very high susceptibility zones were distributed in Kawabaiqing Town, Lagen Town, and Yupu Town. High susceptibility zones were distributed in Tongmai-Guxiang Town, Songzong-Yupu Town, the area between Ranwu and Jida Town, and Baima Town. Moderate susceptibility zones were distributed in the west of Zhamu Town. Low susceptibility zones were distributed in the east of Gu Town and Ranwu Town. Very low susceptibility zones were distributed in Jida Town and the east of Zhamu Town.

papers.title: Research on the Residual Strength Characteristics of Landslide Slip Zone Soil in Reservoir Areas Based on Ring Shear Testing
papers.summary: The sliding zone soil constitutes a critical stratum governing landslide stability, rendering it essential for investigating the initiation mechanisms and conducting stability assessments of reservoir-induced landslides. Nevertheless, existing research on the residual shear strength of sliding zone soils in such landslides remains limited. To address this gap, this study focuses on the sliding zone soil sampled from the Xuwa landslide and employs ring shear testing to systematically characterize its residual strength behavior under varying moisture conditions. Test results reveal that specimen failure is consistently manifested as concentric circular scratches centered on the annular shear surface. Specifically, at low moisture contents, the scratches are deeper, and the failure surface exhibits pronounced roughness, abundant asperities, and thin, fragmented material; conversely, at high moisture contents, the scratches become shallower, the failure surface smoothens significantly, asperities diminish, and fragments become thicker and more cohesive. Furthermore, an evident transition in deformation behavior is observed, from strain-softening to strain-hardening, with increasing moisture content. These findings contribute valuable experimental insights and serve as a reference for advancing the understanding and modeling of residual strength in reservoir landslide sliding zone soils.

papers.title: Monitoring Earthflow Displacements Using UAV Surveys and Offset Tracking Techniques: Case Studies from the Northern Apennines, Italy
papers.summary: Landslides represent one of the most widespread and impactful natural hazards, and their monitoring remains a key issue for risk assessment and mitigation. In recent years, multi-temporal Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) surveys have become an important data source for landslide monitoring, enabling detection of surface changes through repeated acquisitions. This study proposes a fully UAV-based workflow to quantify planar displacements of active, moderately rapid earthflows using multi-temporal Light Detection and Ranging (LiDAR) and optical data. The approach is tested on two landslides in the northern Apennines (Italy): the Sassi Neri and Antognano landslides, with different activity trends and geomorphological maturity. Three UAV campaigns were conducted for each landslide. Surface displacements were estimated using an automated offset tracking approach implemented through the SenseTrack algorithm, based on Digital Image Correlation applied to UAV-derived hillshade. The reliability of offset tracking results was validated through Homologous Point Tracking, based on manual tracking of surface objects and features on orthomosaics and hillshades. Displacement maps reveal a well-defined deformation pattern at Sassi Neri, whereas the Antognano landslide shows a more heterogeneous and discontinuous displacement distribution. Quantitative comparison between automated and manual measurements shows strong agreement for both case studies, with R² values of 0.92 for Sassi Neri and 0.93 for Antognano. These results demonstrate that multi-temporal UAV surveys combined with offset tracking provide accurate estimates of planar displacements from decimetric to multi-metric magnitudes. The proposed workflow is a rapid, flexible, and cost-effective solution for short- to medium-term landslide monitoring, particularly for emergency scenarios and areas where ground-based instrumentation is unviable.

papers.title: Internal Erosion in Colluvial Gravelly Soil Under Different Rainfall Intensities and Its Effects on Water Migration and Soil Structure
papers.summary: Rainfall infiltration commonly triggers shallow landslides by raising pore-water pressure and reducing shear strength. This mechanism, however, presupposes that the soil structure remains stable. In colluvial slopes composed of gravelly soils, rainfall infiltration may induce the migration of fine particles, a phenomenon known as internal erosion that alters the soil structure and consequently affects slope stability. To investigate internal erosion in colluvial gravelly soil under different rainfall intensities and its effects on water migration and soil structural characteristics, a series of laboratory soil column tests were conducted using a self-designed rainfall infiltration apparatus. The wetting front migration, soil moisture evolution, and fine-particle outflow under five rainfall intensities (30, 60, 90, 120, and 150 mm/h), together with the changes in grain-size distribution and pore structure before and after the tests, were systematically analyzed. The results indicate that rainfall intensity exerted a markedly layer-dependent influence on the infiltration process of colluvial gravelly soil: the steady-state moisture content increased most markedly in the upper layer and moderately in the lower layer but remained almost unchanged in the middle layer. Under the present test conditions, a rainfall intensity threshold of 30–60 mm/h was identified for the onset of fine-particle mobilization. Below this threshold, no particle washout occurred. Once it was exceeded, the effluent fine-particle concentration exhibited an initial peak followed by a later-stage decline, and the cumulative eroded mass increased with rainfall intensity. The vertical distribution of particle loss was closely aligned with the moisture content response across layers. The image-estimated porosity change rate at the front face of the soil column increased with rainfall intensity. It was negative under low-intensity rainfall, with values of −5.07% and −4.63% at 30 and 60 mm/h. At higher

papers.title: Probabilistic Landslide Assessment in a Changing Climate: Insight from Multi-Hazard Interactions
papers.summary: Landslides are expected to become more frequent and severe under climate change. At climate-change time scales, slopes are subjected to repeated exposure to multiple hazards (e.g., rainfall and earthquakes) in many regions. However, long-term landslide assessment under multiple hazards remains a major challenge, owing to the distinct characteristics of hazard occurrence, the nonstationarity introduced by climate change, as well as the complex interactions between these different hazards affecting slope stability. This study proposes a probabilistic multi-hazard framework for assessing landslides under rainfall and seismic hazards in a changing climate, based on stochastic renewal process theory. An illustrative example is provided for a representative slope to demonstrate the applicability of the proposed framework. The results indicate that neglecting the interactions between rainfall and seismic hazards lead to a substantial underestimation of long-term landslide probability. Moreover, the impact of climate change on landslide probability is highly dependent on the relative dominance of climate-sensitive hazards (i.e., rainfall) within the multi-hazard system in the analyzed region.

papers.title: Temperature Evolution in Sandy Soil Under Large-Displacement Shear
papers.summary: Granular material within the sliding zone of a landslide can undergo large-displacement shearing during its motion. The mechanical behaviour of the material under such shear process significantly affects the basal friction of a landslide and therefore governs its mobility. Both field observations and laboratory experiments have provided evidence that this shear process is companied by significant temperature generation. The generated heat can dynamically modify the shear strength of the material by degrading organic matter or influencing pore pressure. Although the effects of shear-induced temperature rise have been discussed in previous studies, it remains difficult to directly record the temperature evolution during large-displacement shearing. In this study, a direct temperature measurement unit integrated with a ring-shear apparatus is developed to record the complete temperature evolution process, from heating to cooling. Ring-shear tests were conducted on silica sand samples with two different grain sizes. The results indicate that the temperature evolution curve exhibits an initial increase followed by a steady rising phase once the specimen reaches the critical state. With continued shearing, the temperature generation rate gradually decreases, which is attributed to grain crushing occurring within the shear zone. The measurements further reveal a pronounced spatial heterogeneity in temperature distribution along the shear zone, with the temperature at the centre being approximately four times higher than that near the boundary. These obtained data are expected to be valuable for calibrating parameters in thermal-mechanically coupled numerical analyses of landslide dynamics.

papers.title: Impacts of rainfall variability on landslide stability revealed by PS-InSAR and numerical modeling: a case study of the Xincun Landslide, Baode County, China
papers.summary: No abstract available

papers.title: Mobility of dry granular flows over contrasting erodible bed materials in laboratory experiments
papers.source: Natural hazards and earth system sciences
papers.summary: Abstract. Debris-flow mobility responds sensitively to erosion and entrainment that exchange mass and momentum across the flow-bed interface. Yet, the mechanical controls that cause some debris flows to accelerate during erosion while others decelerate are insufficiently understood. Recent theory attributes this divergent behavior to inertial contrasts between the moving mass and the erodible bed, suggesting that incorporating inertially weaker, neutral, or stronger substrate into the flow enhances, maintains, or reduces flow mobility, respectively. Here, we conducted flume experiments and surface-based measurements to assess how the inertia of the erodible bed affects the flow kinematics, erosion, entrainment, and runout of dry granular single-phase debris flows. We systematically imposed inertial contrasts by releasing a quartz slide of constant solid density over erodible beds with lower, equal, and higher solid densities representing inertially weak, neutral, and strong scenarios, and compare these alongside a reference case without erosion. Each scenario was repeated for fine sand and a sand-gravel mixture. Our results reveal consistent behavior across both particle-size distributions. Debris flows over low-density beds exhibit higher apparent mean erosion rates, faster flow fronts before deposition, and longer runout lengths, whereas flows over equal- and high-density beds evolve similarly, with shallower erosion, slower flow fronts, and shorter, more compact deposits. Relative to the neutral scenario, the entrainment of low-density material thus appears to enhance debris-flow mobility, while incorporating high-density material does not lead to the anticipated mobility loss. This asymmetric response suggests that solid-density contrasts alone are insufficient to explain the observed trends under the experimental conditions considered here. papers.title: Experimental data on the flow evolution and deposit morphology of dry granular flows over contrasting erodible bed materials
papers.summary: Gravity-driven mass movements are highly dynamic events in which the erosion and entrainment of basal sediment can greatly enhance flow mobility and energy, extending travel distances and intensifying impact forces. However, the underlying physical conditions and mechanical controls that cause some erosive flows to accelerate while others decelerate are still insufficiently understood, and predicting these dynamics accurately with existing empirical models remains challenging. This data publication supplements the study on the mobility of dry granular flows over contrasting erodible beds by Wetterauer et al. (2026), which investigates how systematically imposed flow-bed contrasts influence the mobility and runout of dry erosive granular flows using controlled laboratory experiments. A total of 24 dry granular flow experiments were conducted in a steep flume, testing four distinct slide-bed configurations called “scenarios”. These include three erosive scenarios representing low-density, equal-density, and high-density conditions, achieved by systematically varying the solid particle density of the bed material (expanded glass, quartz, and magnetite) relative to a sliding mass (quartz) of constant solid particle density. For reference, the fourth scenario is without an erodible bed. Each scenario was performed for a finer (sand-sized) and a coarser (sand-to-gravel-sized) particle fraction to assess potential grain-size-dependent effects and repeated three times to evaluate reproducibility. Here, we provide high-resolution spatiotemporal data on the flow evolution and deposit morphology for all 24 experiments together with information on the material properties of slide and bed. The data were collected as part of the project “Landslide mobility with erosion: Proof-of-concept and application”, which investigates entrainment processes and their effects on the mobility of erosive flows based on dry granular flow experiments and debris-flow experiments. papers.title: Malawi Multimodal Earth Observation Dataset for Landslide Mapping Following Cyclone Freddy 2023.
papers.source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.summary: This dataset provides a multimodal Earth Observation dataset developed for deep-learning-based landslide mapping following Cyclone Freddy in Malawi. The data are organized into 128 × 128 pixel patches at 3 m spatial resolution and include landslide ground-truth masks together with topographic and Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) information used in the associated deep-learning experiments. The dataset is divided into training, validation, and independent test subsets containing 1,536, 171, and 382 patches, respectively. The test subset includes both landslide-positive and landslide-negative samples. The distributed modalities include the landslide masks; DEM-derived terrain information, including elevation, slope, aspect, curvature, flow accumulation, and flow direction; and Sentinel-1 SAR products, including pre-event and post-event VV/VH data and coherence layers. PlanetScope optical data: PlanetScope-derived RGB, NIR, and NDVI patches used in the study are not redistributed with this dataset because of Planet imagery licensing restrictions. Instead, patch-level metadata required for optical reconstruction are provided in PlanetScope_post_source_per_patch.csv. Users who have their own authorized Planet account and the necessary imagery access can reconstruct the corresponding RGB, NIR, and NDVI patches using the Malawi_PlanetScope_Exact_Patch_Rebuilder.ipynb notebook provided in the associated GitHub repository. The workflow uses the exact spatial footprint and acquisition information for each patch, retrieves the corresponding PlanetScope Surface Reflectance imagery through the Planet APIs, and reconstructs the optical layers on the dataset grid. The associated GitHub repository also provides the training and independent-test inference notebooks for the dual-branch SegFormer MiT-B2 framework used with RGB, pre-event VV coherence, and post-event VV coherence inputs. papers.title: Recycling of coal mining waste geomaterials as a construction material
papers.summary: Much of the existing knowledge surrounding colliery discards dates back to the 1970s and 1980s, largely developed in response to the Aberfan disaster of 1966. However, the advancement of soil mechanics, both in theoretical frameworks and experimental methods, necessitates a renewed examination of these geomaterials. To fill this gap, samples of coal mine waste geomaterials (CMWG) were collected from the RH01 site located in Tylorstown, Wales. An experimental programme was designed to investigate physical, mineralogical, chemical, hydraulic, mechanical, and unsaturated properties of the CMWG. The main research objectives are: (a) examine the role of particle breakage, particularly initial breakage, on their mechanical response, (b) assess the effect of cementation on their properties and shearing response, (c) understand the instability and failure mechanisms of the geomaterials under a constant deviatoric shear (CDS) path (d) evaluate the suitability of the geomaterials as a construction material, particularly as a potential replacement for sand in construction, and (e) Assess feasibility of using produced concrete as a capillary barrier for mitigating geohazards during intense rainfall events. Key findings from this study can be summarised as: i) Tylorstown CMWG (TCMWG) is a highly crushable geomaterial, with particle breakage occurring during compaction, consolidation, and shearing. Initial breakage introduced during compaction influences both drained and undrained responses; however, addition of cement enhances its properties, such as stiffness (Young’s modulus) and shear strength, ii) onset of instability under a CDS path is strongly influenced by drainage conditions and unloading rate as well as initial breakage, (iii) TCMWG demonstrated to have the capacity to completely replace sand. TCMWG’s crushing characteristic gives higher ductility, while comparing to sand, it demands higher 𝑤𝑒𝑓𝑓𝑐⁄, and (iv) shotcrete pad made from TCMWG can delay water infiltration int

papers.title: A physics-informed neural network-based computational method for forward and inverse analysis of buried pipelines subjected to lateral landslides
papers.summary: Buried oil and gas pipelines in mountainous regions are frequently subjected to transverse landslide loading, necessitating accurate forward mechanical prediction and reliable inverse load identification for structural safety evaluation. Conventional finite element methods serve as the standard tool for forward analysis of such structures, yet they inherently lack the capability to assimilate sparse field monitoring data—a critical prerequisite for quantifying unknown landslide-induced loads. Although physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) offer unified forward–inverse modeling capacity, their practical application to large-scale pipeline problems is limited by inherent spectral bias, stringent strong-form continuity requirements, and automatic differentiation overhead. This study proposes a domain-decomposed energy-based PINN framework for Winkler-supported pipeline beams, adopting single-hidden-layer networks with cubic Hermite interpolation, analytical differentiation, and a weak-form energy loss functional. The established framework supports both single-stage static load identification via bilevel optimization and Tikhonov regularization, as well as two-stage time-varying load evolution tracking through dual-network temporal coupling. Benefiting from the unified PINN architecture, heterogeneous monitoring data including deflection, rotation, and strain measurements can be flexibly fused across staged monitoring procedures. Forward validation against ABAQUS benchmarks under both cosine and asymmetric ridge load distributions yields relative errors below 0.2% for deflection, rotation, bending moment, and strain. Inverse tests for both load patterns demonstrate that deflection-based monitoring achieves high-accuracy load reconstruction (RMSE <80 kN / m ) with five or more sensors, and two-stage incremental monitoring effectively refines time-varying load amplitude estimation, albeit constrained by the baseline accuracy of initial sparse inversion. papers.title: Assessment and Mapping of Soil Erosion Hotspots in the Himalayan Region Using RUSLE and Machine Learning Technique
papers.summary: Soil erosion is a major driver of land degradation, particularly in fragile and ecologically sensitive mountainous regions such as the Himalayas. This study assessed soil erosion risk and mapped erosion hotspots in the Bhagirathi watershed, Uttarkashi District, Uttarakhand, by integrating the Revised Universal Soil Loss Equation (RUSLE), remote sensing, GIS, field observations, and Random Forest (RF) machine learning. The assessment utilized 80 spatially distributed surface soil samples for estimating soil erodibility, ALOS PALSAR DEM (12.5 m) for terrain characterization and derivation of topographic factors, and Sentinel-2A multispectral data (10 m) for land use/land cover and spectral information. Rainfall, soil, topographic, vegetation, and management-related factors were integrated within the RUSLE framework to estimate soil loss, while terrain and spectral variables were subsequently used to develop the RF regression model. Areas experiencing estimated soil loss exceeding 40 t ha⁻¹ yr⁻¹ were classified as erosion hotspots. The RUSLE-based erosion risk assessment showed good agreement with field observations, achieving an overall validation accuracy of 85%. The RF regression model demonstrated good predictive performance, with an R² of 0.72, RMSE of 0.31, and Nash–Sutcliffe Efficiency of 0.67. Slope, aspect and NDVI were found to be the most important predictors governing the model performance as well as spatial distribution of erosion hotspots. Erosion hotspots occupied approximately 9.34% of the watershed and were predominantly associated with steep slopes and areas with sparse or absent vegetation. These locations were also clearly identifiable in high-resolution satellite imagery. The findings demonstrate that integrating empirical erosion modelling with field observations, geospatial data, and machine learning can effectively assess erosion risk and identify priority hotspots in complex and inaccessible Himalayan terrain. papers.title: LCRA predicts event-aligned canopy responses across unseen Qinling landscapes
papers.summary: Introduction Predicting event-aligned canopy variation in mountains requires integrating vegetation state, phenology, irregular satellite observations, and landform context. We asked whether a task-structured predictor could improve spatial transfer of short-horizon EVI responses across unseen Qinling landscapes. Methods We studied 80 response-blind matched sets in the Qinling Mountains, each comprising one mapped landform and two same-event non-landslide controls, yielding 991 set-events and 2,973 member responses across 32 spatial blocks. The landform-conditioned canopy response aggregator (LCRA) integrated dated MODIS EVI with climate-season, terrain, canopy-state summaries, and matched-member relations to predict subsequent-minus-pre-event (S-P) and subsequent-minus-impact (S-I) EVI. Models were evaluated with block-exclusive outer folds, and nominal composite-start-window results were compared with a complete 16-day support analysis. Results In the nominal analysis, the compact LCRA core ensemble achieved member R 2 = 0.8219 versus 0.7964 for the EVI-state-plus-season linear reference Δ R 2 = +0.0254; 95%; block × shared-onset interval 0.0037−0.0532; matched-contrast R 2 was comparable (0.3684 versus 0.3677). Requiring complete 16-day input support to end before the target window yielded member R 2 = 0.7810 in 80 sets and 0.7988 in all 90 eligible sets; in the latter, Δ R 2 versus linear was +0.0240 −0.0037 to 0.0547), while MAE decreased by 0.0041 EVI (0.0002–0.0087). Validation-based variance scaling reduced primary-task 95% interval width by 38.6% and brought empirical coverage from 99.4% to 92.9%, with improved probabilistic scores. Observed responses showed seasonal sign reversal: mean S-P was +0.0710 EVI in May–June and −0.1814 and −0.1849 in July–August and September. papers.title: Scientific Mapping and Scientometric Evaluation of Geospatial Technologies in Landslide Research: Trends, Collaboration Networks, and Emerging Research Directions
papers.summary: Landslides remain one of the most frequent and destructive natural hazards globally, significantly influenced by climate change, rapid urbanization, deforestation, and unplanned developmental activities. In response, geospatial technologies such as Remote Sensing (RS), Geographic Information Systems (GIS), Light Detection and Ranging (LiDAR), Interferometric Synthetic Aperture Radar (InSAR), Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) and machine learning techniques have increasingly been applied to improve landslide prediction, monitoring, susceptibility mapping, and disaster risk reduction. This study presents a bibliometric evaluation of global research trends related to geospatial technologies in landslide studies during the period 2000–2025. A total of 14,909 publications indexed in Web of Science and Scopus were analysed using the bibliometrix package in R. The analysis identified 2,385 publication sources and an annual scientific growth rate of 14.64%, indicating the rapid expansion of research activities in the field. The study examined publication trends, citation impact, thematic evolution, keyword structure, and international collaboration patterns. The results revealed substantial growth in scientific production, particularly after 2018, driven by advances in spatial data acquisition, artificial intelligence integration, and increasing global disaster risk awareness. China, Italy, India, and the United States emerged as the leading contributors to the research domain. Keyword and thematic analyses demonstrated a clear transition from conventional geomorphological and mapping-based approaches toward advanced machine learning-driven predictive modelling and geospatial monitoring frameworks. The study further identified two major interconnected research streams: remote sensing-based monitoring and GIS-based susceptibility modelling. papers.title: Depth-Averaged Modelling of Earthquake-Triggered Submarine Landslides on Continental Margins and Canyon Terrains
papers.source: Journal of Marine Science and Engineering
papers.summary: Infrastructure located on the seabed is vulnerable to earthquake-triggered submarine landslides, although the propagation of failure and the post-seismic movement of slides on the continental margin or in a submarine canyon have not been well interpreted. A three-dimensional depth-averaged method was used to revisit the initiation, progressive failure, and runout of two typical scenarios: a back-analysis of the deep-seated Ashton Seamount landslide and a scenario prediction in a canyon system in the South China Sea. For the former, the shear band is propagated extensively through a weak layer prior to the slab failure of thick overlying sediment. The influence of soil sensitivity on initial co-seismic softening may be insignificant, while it severely affects the subsequent shear band propagation and runout. The ratio of the affected area approaches six as soil sensitivity is increased from two to five. In the canyon system, several fully softened regions may be caused independently on steep canyon flanks. These regions are then progressively expanded and merged during the earthquake. The sliding masses move along several canyon channels before converging at the gully junctions. Sediment downslope is removed during the initial slope failure, thereby impairing the support provided to the upslope sediment and suggesting more retrogressive failures even after the earthquake. As a result, a peak velocity of 40.8 m/s and an affected area of 23.4 km2 are predicted.

papers.title: Physical Structure Overrides Short‐Term Nitrogen Effects on Preferential Flow in Heterogeneous Rock‐Soil Media: Implications for Mountain Ecohydrology
papers.summary: ABSTRACT Mountainous critical zones, with heterogeneous rock‐soil structures, regulate water storage and flux through complex subsurface flow paths. Preferential flow, often triggered by textural contrasts, controls rapid water redistribution and eco‐hydrological connectivity. This study investigates the divergent infiltration dynamics between two dominant media—coarse, weathered clastic rock and finer brown soil—in the Taihang Mountains through controlled column experiments under varied nitrogen (N) concentrations (0–125 mg N L −1 ). A quantitative multi‐criteria framework was applied to discriminate matrix flow from preferential flow, including volume‐balance closure via the piston displacement index ( ν ), velocity ratio, flux‐capacity ratio, wetting‐front morphology with Monte Carlo noise calibration, and Green–Ampt consistency. Brown soil was matrix‐dominated ( ν * = 0.93–1.12; smooth wetting fronts) and retained significantly more water, with cumulative infiltration of 18.1–21.8 cm and effective storage capacity of 19.4 cm over the 45‐cm profile. Clastic rock exhibited strong bypass behaviour ( ν * = 1.35–1.53; p = 0.005), with 26%–35% of infiltrated water moving beyond the visible wetting front, despite its late‐time flux remaining below the matrix saturated conductivity. Cumulative infiltration in clastic rock was significantly lower (13.3–15.2 cm; p = 0.005), and its leaching risk index was medium‐to‐high (0.44–0.88) compared with low values in brown soil (0.08–0.24; p = 0.002). Wetting front velocity was significantly higher in clastic rock in all phases (), but morphology remained near‐piston‐like (), indicating that rapid infiltration was a matrix‐capacity and storage‐capacity effect rather than finger‐like preferential flow. Nitrogen addition, applied as a short‐term chemical perturbation, did not significantly alter these physical controls across the tested range. These findings provide a mechanistic basis for understanding water partitioning, retentio

papers.title: Spatial Block-Evaluated Graph Neural Networks for Landslide Susceptibility Mapping in North Kashkadarya, Uzbekistan
papers.summary: Landslide susceptibility mapping in spatially clustered mountain terrain requires models that represent spatial dependence and geographically structured evaluation.This study compared five graph neural network (GNN) architectures for North Kashkadarya, Uzbekistan: graph convolutional network (GCN), Graph Sample and Aggregate (GraphSAGE), relational graph convolutional network (R-GCN), Chebyshev graph convolutional network (ChebNet), and a TransformerConv graph neural network (TransformerConv GNN) that does not implement the full Graphormer architecture.An inventory of 272 mapped landslide features was converted to 900 presence samples and paired with 900 distance-constrained absence samples.Twenty-one geological, topographic, hydrological, and environmental factors were harmonized at 20 m.Hyperparameters were selected within nested spatial block cross-validation, and performance was summarized using receiver operating characteristic-area under the curve (ROC-AUC), precision-recall-area under the curve (PR-AUC), F1, and Brier score.R-GCN produced the highest observed scores (ROC-AUC = 0.9383, PR-AUC = 0.9401, F1 = 0.8778, Brier score = 0.1033), followed by ChebNet.The five model-specific susceptibility maps consistently emphasized the dissected eastern and northeastern mountain belts, although class boundaries varied among architectures.Integrated-gradient attribution ranked northness, normalized difference vegetation index (NDVI), downslope curvature, geomorphons, and terrain-surface texture as the leading model controls.The results support GNN-based regional susceptibility screening, while the transductive graph, unbuffered block design, static inventory, and 1 km prediction-node spacing limit claims of external generalization or site-scale prediction.

papers.title: Reproducibility package: class-agnostic candidate generation and calendar-derived event windows for rapid landslide mapping
papers.source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.summary: Code, data definitions, per-image scores and result artefacts behind the manuscript Class-agnostic candidate generation and calendar-derived event windows for rapid landslide mapping, released on top of version 1.0.0 of the same repository (which documented the earlier journal version). What the archive contains. scripts/ implements the Event-Bracketing Rule (f1_calendar_rule.py), the discovery baselines, the training-free separability criterion (LOFO and baseline variants) and the paired bootstrap. data/ holds the per-tile acquisition calendar (dates.jsonl), the per-tile separability features (features_15f.jsonl) and the derived-data definitions for the eight arm configurations. results/json/ holds every metric reported in the paper, results/per_image/ the per-image score arrays from which the paired confidence intervals are recomputed, results/logs/ the training and evaluation logs with the chain scripts, and results/run_configs/ the per-run configuration and test metrics. figures/ holds the published figures with their plotting scripts, and figures/ghnr/ the builders for the figure set used in this version. CHECKSUMS.sha256 together with verify_checksums.py allows every file to be verified before use. Model checkpoints (33 GB) and the Sen12Landslides imagery (57 GB) are not included; both are described in the README and can be regenerated or downloaded (Hoehn et al. 2025, https://huggingface.co/datasets/paulhoehn/Sen12Landslides).

papers.title: Hybrid deep learning approach for predicting long-term deformation of landslides
papers.summary: Actively moving landslides threaten life, property, and infrastructure. While monitoring movement velocity is essential for understanding landslide processes, predicting deformation magnitude is a significant step toward mitigation. This study develops a hybrid deep learning model integrating a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN), a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network, and attention mechanisms to predict landslide-related ground deformation from spatial and temporal data. The model was developed for areas of Central Italy heavily affected by the 2016–2017 seismic events, using a three-way experimental protocol. Temporal data comprise Persistent Scatterer (PS) observations for 2018–2022, whereas spatial data represent landslide predisposing factors. The CNN extracts spatial features associated with landslide susceptibility, while the LSTM captures temporal dependencies in cumulative deformation. Attention mechanisms further refine the model by weighting critical regions and time steps. On an independent hold-out test set, not used for hyperparameter tuning or model selection, the model achieved low prediction errors for both ascending and descending geometries, and the close agreement between training, validation, and test results indicates limited overfitting. Overall, the proposed CNN-LSTM-attention framework provides a transferable, InSAR-driven basis for anticipating where and when landslide deformation is likely to intensify, supporting hazard zonation, monitoring prioritisation, and early-warning strategies in seismically active regions.

papers.title: Knowledge-graph reasoning for temporal lag effects and mechanism inversion of heavy-rainfall-induced landslide events: case study on Hong Kong
papers.summary: Heavy rainfall can sustain landslide activity for several days after a storm, but daily event inventories often obscure this delayed response and provide little information on the evidence used to infer failure processes. We developed a knowledge-graph workflow that links 2,961 Hong Kong landslide records from 2001 to 2021 with daily rainfall, slope attributes, spatial relations, and 57 investigation reports. Lag analysis was possible for 2,950 records, mechanism analysis for 2,940 records, and 43 events had traceable report anchors. Daily incidence rates and threshold–window tests identified a high-hazard stage on days 0–3 and an extended-hazard stage on days 4–7. With a 50 mm threshold and a 7 days look-back window, 42.2% of events occurred on a qualifying rainfall day and 30.1% occurred during the following week. A nearest-station test using 21 gauges produced 89.4% agreement with the baseline stage classification. The graph combined storm, slope-form, neighborhood, and regional evidence to estimate five mechanism classes. Pore-pressure-dominated soil slides and channelized debris flows accounted for 78.9%–84.4% of classifications across lag stages, while posterior uncertainty increased with lag. Leakage-controlled leave-one-out testing yielded Top-1 and Top-2 accuracies of 0.163 and 0.349. These results support storm-cluster interpretation and investigation prioritization, while event-specific causes still require field evidence.

papers.title: Assessing the Influence of Land Use Change Pattern and Soil Erosion on Sediment Delivery Ratio in the Upper Mahaweli River Catchment of Sri Lanka
papers.summary: The Mahaweli River takes in the largest volume of water amounting to one seventh of Sri Lanka’s total runoff and has a catchment area that covers 15 % of the land in the country. A number of multipurpose reservoirs have been stored in the Upper Mahaweli River Catchment (UMRC) mainly to generate hydropower, which contributes to about 40-50% of the total hydropower production in the country. This study investigates the impacts of land use change patterns and soil erosion on the sediment delivery ratio (SDR) within the UMRC in Sri Lanka. Utilizing Geographic Information Systems (GIS) and Remote Sensing (RS) tools, the land use and land cover (LULC) changes were analyzed over a period from 2007 to 2023, focusing on soil erosion's contribution to sediment dynamics in the basin. By employing the Universal Soil Loss Equation (USLE) model, factors such as rainfall erosivity, soil erodibility, slope characteristics, crop cover, and land management practices were assessed to estimate soil loss and map erosion hotspots. The InVEST SDR model was then applied to quantify sediment transport and deposition patterns, helping to identify priority areas for soil conservation. Results revealed an average annual soil loss ranging from 0 to 95.015 t ha⁻¹ yr⁻¹ in the catchment and a mean annual sediment export of 5.56 t ha⁻¹ yr⁻¹. It shows mean sediment deposition rate as 2.4 t ha⁻¹ yr⁻¹. Erosion severity was classified into five hazard classes, very low (0 - 5 t ha-1 yr-1), low (5 - 10 t ha-1 yr -1), moderate (10 - 20 t ha-1 yr-1), high (20 - 50 t ha-1 yr-1) and very high ( >50 t ha-1 yr -1). A critical 1.5% area was identified as a considerable soil erosion hazard area, necessitating urgent measures for erosion control. Findings indicate significant LULC changes, driven primarily by deforestation, agricultural expansion, and urbanization, which have intensified mean soil erosion rate from 2.39 t ha-1 yr-1to 11.22 t ha-1 yr-1, highest mean sediment export rate as 2.29 t ha-1 yr-1 and hi

papers.title: Adaptive Prototype‐Based Few‐Shot Segmentation for Debris Flow Early Warning
papers.summary: ABSTRACT Debris flows are highly destructive geohazards requiring rapid, accurate perception for effective early warning and emergency response. However, deep learning methods depend heavily on large datasets, whereas debris flow imagery is inherently scarce. Although few‐shot semantic segmentation (FSS) addresses data limitations, existing methods suffer from semantic ambiguity and weak adaptability to complex target morphologies. To address these challenges, this study proposes a cross‐modal few‐shot segmentation framework and constructs a visible‐light benchmark dataset named DebrisFlow‐VisSeg (DFVS). The framework incorporates a Cross‐Modal Feature Enhancement Unit (CFEU) to improve visual‐semantic discrimination, an Adaptive Prototype Construction Mechanism (APCM) to generate robust prototypes for heterogeneous structures, and a Query Feature Disentanglement and Alignment Module (QF‐DAM) to suppress background interference. Extensive experiments on DFVS, PASCAL‐5 i , and COCO‐20 i demonstrate that the method outperforms state‐of‐the‐art approaches. Specifically, it achieves 76.31% mIoU under the 1‐shot setting and 80.97% mIoU under the 5‐shot setting on DFVS. Field deployment further verifies its practical applicability for real‐world debris flow monitoring under data‐scarce conditions.

papers.title: From Hazard Maps to Decision Intelligence: A Critical Review of GIS, Remote Sensing and GeoAI for Disaster Risk Management and Engineering Resilience
papers.source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.summary: Disaster risk is inherently spatial, yet geographic information systems (GIS) are still frequently used to end analysis at a classified hazard map rather than to support an engineering or operational decision. This critical review traces how GIS, integrated with remote sensing (RS), multi-criteria decision analysis (MCDA), Web-GIS and geospatial artificial intelligence (GeoAI), has evolved across the disaster management cycle, and evaluates whether the resulting products are validated, uncertainty-aware and usable in civil-engineering practice. Twenty foundational studies (1992–2017) covering general emergency management, floods, earthquakes, landslides, cyclones and coastal hazards, drought and forest fire are appraised against a structured set of dimensions and are updated with recent systematic reviews of Web-GIS, AI/ML-enabled GIS, drone-based hazard sensing and AI-based landslide analysis. Four analytical families (knowledge-driven, data-driven, simulation-based and integrated Web-GIS/GeoAI) are compared. Knowledge-driven methods such as AHP and weighted overlay remain valuable where event inventories are scarce but are sensitive to expert-assigned weights; statistical and machine-learning models can improve prediction but are vulnerable to spatial leakage, non-representative inventories and limited interpretability; operational Web-GIS and GeoAI systems are advancing quickly but are rarely validated against independent events or evaluated by their effect on decisions. The most persistent gap is the translation of hazard classes into engineering quantities such as flood depth and velocity, design ground motion, slope safety factors, damage states and lifeline reliability. The review proposes (i) an eight-stage data-to-decision framework linking GIS, RS, GeoAI and engineering analysis, (ii) a minimum reporting and validation checklist for GIS-based hazard studies, and (iii) a prioritised research agenda covering multi-hazard modelling, near-real-time Web-GIS, un

papers.title: Integrating Multi-Temporal Sentinel-1 InSAR, GIS-Based Susceptibility Modeling, and Geotechnical Monitoring for Sustainable Dam Safety: Capabilities and Limits at the Yaprak Dam Reservoir, Türkiye
papers.summary: Reservoir slope instability threatens the safe and sustainable operation of dams. This study tests what open access data can reveal about a reactivated landslide on the left-bank reservoir slope of the Yaprak I Dam (Amasya, Türkiye) by combining multi-temporal Sentinel-1 InSAR, SAR-derived reservoir surface area, a GIS-based weighted overlay susceptibility model, and site-investigation data. Ascending and descending 2017–2024 interferograms were inverted with a small-baseline approach and decomposed into vertical and east–west components. In the instrumented sector, mean line-of-sight velocities ranged from −1.1 to +1.6 mm/yr and the east–west component was about −2 mm/yr, all below the local detection threshold of about 5 mm/yr (2σ). This agrees with the 2.8–7.9 mm recorded by six inclinometers over 4–12 months in 2022–2023, whereas the 20.6–24.9 mm recorded by two older casings in July–November 2022 were not resolved. Correlations between reservoir surface area and displacement were not significant after correction for multiple testing, and InSAR anomalies were distributed among susceptibility classes in proportion to their area, irrespective of the factor weights. Open access InSAR thus bounds east–west and vertical slope motion at a few millimetres per year at low cost, but is insensitive to north–south and small-scale movements and cannot replace in situ monitoring.

papers.title: Two large unstable slopes in West Greenland illustrates an emerging Arctic tsunami hazard
papers.summary: Landslides entering fjords or lakes can generate tsunamis that threaten communities far beyond the source area. Here we document the active deformation of two newly identified unstable slopes within the Uummannaq Fjord system in central West Greenland: a large slope in Karrat Fjord ( ~ 400 million m³) and a smaller yet more imminent, slope in Kangerluarsuk Fjord ( ~ 30 million m³). Both were discovered following the catastrophic 2017 Karrat landslide and tsunami, which prompted closer investigations of the region. Numerical tsunami simulations indicate that a potential collapse of the Karrat unstable slope would produce a tsunami affecting the entire fjord system. The scale, location, and evolving nature of these slopes highlight the vulnerability of remote Arctic regions to landslide-induced tsunamis. Likely driven by permafrost degradation, these slopes represent an emerging hazard expected to worsen with continued Arctic warming. Our findings underscore the importance of the monitoring and risk mitigation efforts by local authorities in these rapidly changing high-latitude environments. Newly identified unstable slopes in central West Greenland highlight the emerging Arctic hazard from landslide-generated tsunamis, potentially linked to ongoing permafrost thaw, according to field observations, remote sensing and numerical modelling analysis.

papers.title: Integrated subsurface screening for bioengineering suitability and erosion control on a tropical cut slope
papers.summary: Tropical cut slopes are highly susceptible to erosion and shallow landslides because intense rainfall interacts with deeply weathered residual soils, yet bioengineering interventions are frequently designed without adequate subsurface characterization.This study aimed to conduct an integrated geological, geophysical, and geotechnical characterization of a tropical cut slope on the Kenny Hill Formation, Selangor, Malaysia, in order to evaluate its suitability for bioengineering.Field reconnaissance and weathering grade classification were combined with a two-dimensional electrical resistivity survey, soil penetration resistance, near-surface moisture content, and erosion rate measurements collected across three vegetation coverage plots over 24 months.The slope was classified as Grade III to IV weathered metasedimentary rock with a sandy clay loam surface texture.Resistivity imaging identified a high resistivity, coarse-textured near-surface layer of 20,000 to 360,000 Ωm at 0 to 5 m depth, overlying a low resistivity, moisture-affected zone of 300 to 800 Ωm at 5 to 14.8 m depth.Penetration resistance increased significantly under vegetation cover, reaching 4.4 kPa in the densely vegetated plot compared with 2.9 kPa in the control, while nearsurface moisture content and hydraulic conductivity rose progressively, and erosion rate declined by up to 74.04% relative to the initial condition.These results indicate that the near-surface zone provides mechanically, hydrologically, and ecologically favorable conditions for root establishment, whereas the deeper zone offers limited support for root anchorage.The corresponding reduction in erosion rate confirms that the subsurface conditions identified through this integrated approach translate into measurable improvement in slope performance.Overall, combining weathering grade classification, resistivity zonation, and penetration resistance testing provides a reliable, fielddeployable framework for screening tropical cut slope

papers.title: Economic and Livelihood Impacts of Meteorological Disasters across Different Climatic Zones of Cameroon: A Mixed-methods Assessment
papers.source: Journal of Geography Environment and Earth Science International
papers.summary: Cameroon experiences recurrent meteorological disasters whose livelihood and economic consequences vary across its major climatic zones. This study assessed common meteorological disasters, their economic and livelihood impacts, and the adaptation strategies used by vulnerable populations in six cities representing four climatic zones. A mixed-methods design combined 1,200 household questionnaires administered in Douala, Tiko, and Bamenda with focus group discussions, key informant interviews, and field observations conducted in Yaoundé, Garoua, and Maroua. Findings showed that floods, landslides, and disease outbreaks were prominent in the Equatorial Cameroon and Equatorial Guinean climatic zones, whereas floods, droughts, dust storms, heatwaves, wildfires, and epidemics were frequently reported in the Sahelian zones. Overall, 65.9% of respondents reported that changing climatic conditions affected their livelihoods. In Douala, 44.1% reported severe property damage and 40.6% severe financial losses, while 38.9% of respondents in Tiko reported severe deterioration in health conditions. Subsistence farmers and livestock keepers were particularly affected through crop damage, livestock losses, reduced yields, and water scarcity. Reported adaptation measures included sandbagging, embankments, relocation, tree planting, livelihood diversification, changes in livestock feed, water management, and traditional housing practices. The findings indicate that meteorological disasters disrupt livelihoods and household economic stability across Cameroon’s climatic zones, while many existing adaptation responses remain only partly effective. Strengthening locally appropriate adaptation, meteorological monitoring, and disaster-risk management may therefore improve resilience in affected communities.

papers.title: Frequency-domain characteristics of shear stress and flow-state transition mechanisms in granular landslides
papers.summary: Abstract The shear response of granular materials is closely related to the initiation and acceleration of geological hazards such as landslides, and it can be described in terms of transitions between jammed-like relaxation and more mobile, inertial rearrangement. To quantify this dynamic process from a frequency-domain perspective, this study combined Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) and Empirical Mode Decomposition (EMD) to analyze shear-stress signals obtained from ring-shear tests on glass beads with different particle sizes. The results showed that the topology of the particle contact network and local inertial effects jointly controlled the frequency distribution of the dominant shear mechanisms. As particle size increased, the energy dissipation mode of the system shifted from low-frequency global cooperative relaxation in finer particles to high-frequency local intermittent rearrangement in coarser particles. In particular, the dimensionless critical frequency increased monotonically with particle size, indicating that particle size is a key factor controlling the threshold of dynamic state transition in granular systems. These findings clarify the role of particle size in cross-scale energy migration within granular systems and demonstrate that the dimensionless critical frequency may serve as a potential physical criterion for distinguishing steady relaxation from inertial rheology. The study therefore provides a new perspective for understanding shear instability in granular materials and offers a potential basis for early warning of geological hazards.

papers.title: Evaluating spatiotemporal variations in landslide susceptibility in Northwest Vietnam
papers.source: International Journal of Environmental Science and Technology
papers.summary: Abstract Torrential rainfall is considered a primary trigger for catastrophic landslide events, which threaten the infrastructure, people, and economy of Vietnam. This study analysed spatiotemporal changes in landslide susceptibility using multitemporal landslide inventories and dynamic predictors, including average annual rainfall, land cover, and NDVI over six years. Landslide susceptibility models for three years were built using extreme gradient boosting (XGB), random forest (RF) and logistic regression (LR) algorithms with multitemporal landslide inventories and 12 predictors. Model performance was evaluated using different spatial block sizes, and a block size of 3,000 m was identified as the optimal configuration, balancing the reduction of spatial autocorrelation with stable predictive performance. The XGB model exhibited the best performance across most validation metrics. SHAP and ALE analyses identified rainfall and elevation as the most important predictors, with landslide probability increasing with annual rainfall up to 1,725 mm and elevation up to 2,000 m. Area of applicability AOA analysis confirmed the XGB model is reliable for producing susceptibility maps across almost the entire study area. Using successive landslide inventories and dynamic predictors retained information from previous events while capturing temporal environmental changes. Although these additions did not result in a continuous improvement in discriminative performance, they contributed to better calibration of the predicted probabilities.
