papers.summary: This repository contains the experimental dataset and R analysis code supporting the research article “Biochar increases penetration resistance despite acidity relief and greater soil moisture in hardsetting soils” by Gholamahmadi et al. The study evaluates the chemical, hydrological, mechanical and vegetation responses of three Portuguese hardsetting pasture soils amended with wood-derived biochar. The experiment combined 18 sloping lysimeters and 18 accompanying pots, with monitoring across one growing season and nine natural rainfall events. The deposited materials support the statistical analyses of soil moisture, penetration resistance, bulk density, vegetation cover, aboveground biomass, runoff, estimated infiltration and soil erosion, including treatment contrasts and associated uncertainty estimates.

papers.title: Hydrological Attributes
papers.summary: The Sundarbans, the world’s largest tidal halophytic mangrove forest, spans 10,200 sq. km across India and Bangladesh, forming a dynamic interface between land and sea. It serves as a critical ecological buffer against cyclones and tidal surges while sustaining millions of people through its rich biodiversity and resources. Groundwater reserves, replenished by rainwater and river infiltration, are vital for drinking water and agricultural needs, though threatened by arsenic contamination and saline intrusion. This deltaic region, fed by the confluence of the Ganga, Brahmaputra, and Meghna rivers, exhibits a complex hydrology shaped by tidal rhythms, freshwater inflows, and rainfall conditions. These unique hydrological processes create a fragile estuarine environment that is highly susceptible to climate change impacts, including sea-level rise, saltwater intrusion, and extreme weather events. Human interventions such as embankments, water diversions, and deforestation further exacerbate the vulnerability of this ecosystem. This chapter explores the intricate hydrological dynamics, challenges posed by environmental changes, and sustainable management strategies to preserve the Sundarbans’ ecological integrity and socio-economic stability.

papers.title: Fuzzy multi criteria decision analysis for drinking water suitability in urban lake groundwater systems in Chennai India
papers.summary: Urban lake–groundwater systems in Chennai, India, face severe contamination challenges due to rapid urbanization, seawater intrusion, and anthropogenic inputs, while conventional water quality assessment approaches often fail to adequately account for uncertainty in ranking outcomes. To address this limitation, the present study applied fuzzy-based multi-criteria decision analysis techniques alongside conventional water quality index and classical multi-criteria decision-making approaches. A total of 30 water samples collected from three major lakes and adjacent groundwater sources were analyzed for physicochemical parameters using standard analytical procedures. The results indicate that lake waters generally comply with drinking water standards, reflecting the beneficial influence of rainfall recharge and dilution processes, whereas groundwater quality is considerably affected by seawater intrusion, prolonged water–rock interaction, and contamination from sewage infiltration and agricultural activities. Hydrogeochemical facies analysis revealed predominantly alkaline waters characterized by calcium–magnesium and sodium–chloride types, while hydrochemical interpretation suggested strong hydraulic connectivity between lakes and adjacent aquifers. Comparative evaluation demonstrated that fuzzy decision-making approaches produced more consistent and uncertainty-aware rankings than conventional methods, thereby providing a more reliable framework for drinking water suitability assessment. The proposed methodology offers a practical and reproducible approach for groundwater quality evaluation in data-limited urban environments and can be applied to similar lake–aquifer systems worldwide. The findings contribute to sustainable water resource management, urban resilience planning, and the achievement of global water sustainability objectives.

papers.title: Assessing Hydrological Impacts of Deforestation and Land Use Change in the Tel River Basin
papers.summary: Land use and land cover changes (LULCC) alter catchment hydrology by changing how water moves between the land surface and the atmosphere. This study examines how land use change between 1985 and 2015 affected the water balance of the Tel River basin, a sub-basin of the Mahanadi system in eastern India. Land cover maps for 1985, 1995, and 2005 were obtained from the national decadal LULC database, and a 2015 map was prepared from Landsat 8 imagery using a Random Forest classifier on Google Earth Engine (GEE) and later validated against NRSC data. The 2015 map reached an overall accuracy of 78.6 % (Kappa 0.68) against independent reference data. Forest and agriculture were mapped reliably, while the smaller classes of built-up land, bare land, and water body were combined into one less reliable category. Hydrological response was simulated with the Variable Infiltration Capacity (VIC) model for 1980 to 2018, using a one-factor-at-a-time design that holds climate constant so that only land use varies. Forest cover fell by 13.02% over the period, with most of the loss going to agriculture (about 1575 km2). With climate held fixed, lower evapotranspiration (about 16 mm/year, or 1.7%) was passed almost entirely into higher surface runoff (about 7 mm, 2.0%) and higher base flow (about 9 mm, 4.6%), while long-term soil water storage stayed essentially unchanged. A pixel-level analysis shows that runoff rises in some parts of the basin and falls in others, so the basin average understates the local change in flood and erosion risk. The results point to the value of catchment-scale water management that accounts for where land use is changing within the basin.

papers.title: Satellite and Reanalysis Soil Moisture Products for Irrigation Monitoring in Northern Algeria
papers.summary: ABSTRACT Accurate estimation of soil moisture (SM) is a critical factor for sustainable irrigation management and food security, especially in semi‐arid agricultural regions where water availability is highly variable. Although reanalysis and satellite‐based products provide extensive spatial coverage, their reliability must be systematically validated against in situ measurements. This study establishes a multi‐product validation benchmark by evaluating and comparing several satellite and model‐based SM products over northern Algeria, including the Soil Water Index from the Advanced Scatterometer (ASCAT), Sentinel‐1 (S1), the SM Active Passive (SMAP) mission, European Centre for Medium‐Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) Reanalysis v5‐Land (ERA5‐Land), and the Global Land Data Assimilation System (GLDAS). The analysis focuses on surface‐to‐near‐surface SM dynamics while accounting for site heterogeneity, product resolution, and sensing‐depth differences. The results reveal pronounced spatial variability linked to local pedoclimatic conditions, including soil properties, vegetation cover, and land‐use characteristics. Across the evaluated sites, ASCAT shows the highest average temporal consistency ( r ≈ 0.84; maximum 0.96 at Chiffa), whereas SMAP shows more balanced performance and Sentinel‐1 exhibits strongly site‐dependent behavior, with local failures discussed in the text. ERA5‐Land effectively reproduces temporal variability ( r up to 0.91), whereas the low unbiased root mean square error (ubRMSE) values obtained for GLDAS indicate a low random error component after bias removal rather than absolute accuracy. The bias profiles show that temporal agreement does not guarantee the absence of systematic error: At Chiffa, biases reach +12.75 percentage points in volumetric SM for ASCAT and +15.40 for ERA5‐Land, whereas the ASCAT bias reaches +14.00 at Oued Smar. The performance observed for ASCAT is specific to the evaluated sites and validation period; it does not cons

papers.title: A Planning Framework for Sustainable Stormwater Management Using Blue–Green Infrastructure in Lublin Streetscapes
papers.summary: Sustainable urban stormwater management requires planning tools that quantify local retention potential while accounting for limited street space and existing infrastructure. This study develops a planning-level framework for selecting and preliminarily sizing blue–green infrastructure (BGI) to support sustainable water and land management in existing streetscapes. A section of Henryka Wolińskiego Street in Lublin, Poland, was divided into 26 sub-catchments. Runoff was estimated from land cover, runoff coefficients, and a 15 min design rainfall depth of 16.13 mm with an annual exceedance probability of 20%, obtained from the PMAXTP model. Rain gardens, infiltration swales, stormwater curb extensions, and bioretention basins were allocated according to spatial, environmental, and infrastructure constraints. Calculated runoff was equivalent to 7.4 mm over the study area. The proposed facilities provided 6.8 mm of design storage and could accommodate 6.6 mm, or 89.4% of calculated runoff, under the adopted assumptions; 0.8 mm, or 10.6%, required sewer discharge. Unused storage coexisted with local deficits, demonstrating the importance of storage location and feasible hydraulic connections. The framework contributes a transparent decision-support procedure for assessing the water-management dimension of urban sustainability through runoff accommodation, residual sewer discharge, and BGI space requirements. These are design estimates, not measured environmental benefits or a comprehensive sustainability assessment. Application elsewhere requires local input data, field verification, and subsequent performance monitoring.

papers.title: GIS-Based Multi-Criteria Analysis for Identifying Suitable Rainwater Harvesting Sites to Enhance Groundwater Recharge: A Case Study of the Western Wellfield in Thaqban Area, Sana’a, Yemen
papers.source: مجلة جامعة صنعاء للعلوم التطبيقية والتكنولوجيا
papers.summary: Groundwater depletion in the Sana’a Basin, Yemen, has intensified due to over-abstraction, rapid urbanization, and limited natural recharge. The Western Wellfield, which supplies a significant portion of Sana’a City’s domestic water demand, has experienced substantial groundwater level declines, highlighting the need for sustainable recharge interventions. This study evaluates the potential of rainwater harvesting (RWH) for enhancing groundwater recharge in the Thaqban area using a Geographic Information System (GIS)-based Multi Criteria Decision Analysis (MCDA) integrated with the Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP). Ten thematic criteria were considered, including rainfall, runoff depth, slope, geological media, soil texture, land use/land cover, drainage density, distance to wadis, distance to groundwater wells, and groundwater depth. The criteria were weighted using AHP and combined through a weighted linear combination (WLC) approach to generate an RWH suitability map. The results show that 1.34% of the study area is highly suitable for RWH implementation, 37.60% is moderately suitable, 58.21% is marginally suitable, and 2.85% is unsuitable. Highly suitable areas are mainly associated with permeable geological formations, favorable topography, and proximity to production wells. This study demonstrates the usefulness of GIS-MCDA techniques for identifying priority recharge zones and supporting sustainable groundwater management in arid environments.

papers.title: Migration and transformation characteristics and potential risk assessment of heavy metals under different rainfall conditions in contaminated soil
papers.summary: Abstract Contaminated mining soils cause heavy metal environmental pollution such as the soil, river, groundwater and plants under rainfall conditions. In this work, the copper, zinc, lead and chromium leaching characteristics, leaching efficiency, fractions variation, binding intensity, mobility and potential environmental risks were investigated under different rainfall conditions. Results demonstrated that Zn obtained a high leaching concentration under the 19.6, 13.1 and 6.5 mL.min −1 , which concentrations were 180.3, 154.7 and 123.5 μg.L −1 , respectively. On the surface soil particles, Cu, Zn, Pb and Cr migrated into the water with the rainwater runoff, indicating a sustainable increase with rainfall intensity raising and obtained a high solubility and mobility, promoting heavy metals to migrate via the soil surface rainwater runoff. Exchangeable and reducible fractions of Pb and Cr have decreased and transformed into the metal ions, which migrated into the outflow, whereas the oxidizable and residual fractions have increased under the rainfall conditions. Cu and Pb obtained more stable fractions, such as the oxidizable and residual fractions. Cu, Zn, Pb and Cr I R values were affected by their concentration and fractions under the rainfall conditions. Heavy metal mobility order was Zn > Pb > Cr > Cu, with M F values of 4.34%, 3.52%, 2.67% and 2.45%, respectively. These results can provide significant support for the mining soils of efficient remediation methods to promote the mines' ecological environmental improvement.

papers.title: Urban Tree Soil Moisture Dynamics Across Central European Cities: A Multi-Site Approach Showing Links Between Hydrology, Tree and Site Characteristics
papers.summary: Abstract. Urban trees face intensifying drought stress, and soil water storage and its dynamics are important for the drought resilience of urban trees. Existing evidence is based on process-based growth and ecosystem-service models, on water-balance studies of urban green spaces and irrigation, and on single-city monitoring campaigns, while multi-city in-situ observations under a consistent methodology are missing. We present a continuously growing database of 555 urban tree sites in 41 Central European locations, each instrumented with soil moisture sensors and paired with meteorological data, topographic, sun exposure and groundwater descriptors, manually digitised land use around the tree and tree characteristics. An event-based workflow detects rain and irrigation events and extracts two response metrics, the normalised soil moisture increase and the drying time. Random Forest models are built for all combinations of target (soil moisture increase, drying time), event type (rain, irrigation) and measurement depth (30, 60, 90 cm). The models explain up to 69 % of the variance of the moisture increase after irrigation and 40 to 55 % for the other combinations in cross-validation. Grouped cross-validation shows that the rain models transfer to unseen sites within 0.03 in R2 while the irrigation models lose 0.21 to 0.37, therefore encoding a site signature of the few heavily irrigating cities. Rain and irrigation responses differ markedly. The mean air temperature during the event and the pre-event rainfall dominate the rain responses, whereas the pre-event soil moisture and the storage capacity of the substrate control the irrigation responses and how long their effect persists. The unsealed, vegetated area around the tree is the only consistently relevant site characteristic, whereas depth to groundwater shows no effect. The database and workflow are openly available and turn the assessment of planting sites and the verification of irrigation into measurable quan

papers.title: Influence of groundwater seasonality on suspended sediment dynamics, in a 20 km 2 Mediterranean mountainous catchment
papers.summary: Abstract. This study investigates the interplay between groundwater and surface runoff in controlling suspended sediment dynamics within the Galabre catchment, a 20 km² Mediterranean mountainous catchment characterized by extensive badland areas. Using an End-Member Mixing Analyzing framework that accounts for event-specific variability in end-member chemistry, the study quantifies surface runoff and groundwater contributions during 86 flood events spanning three hydrological years. Hydrological analyses reveal clear seasonal contrasts in the generation of surface runoff and groundwater flow rates. Surface runoff contributions during floods vary from 0 to 50 % of the instantaneous flow rate, with higher proportions during the dry spring/summer season (May–September) and lower values in autumn/winter. Surface runoff and groundwater flow rates are strongly correlated with event rainfall accumulation, while groundwater-related variables also show sensitivity to antecedent rainfall over 15 days, highlighting their dependence on long-term hydrological connectivity. Results further demonstrate that suspended sediment concentrations correlate more strongly with surface runoff flow rate than with flow rate, emphasizing the dominant role of surface runoff in sediment detachment and transport on hillslopes. Marked seasonal differences in hydrosedimentary processes were observed. Spring/summer floods, driven by short and intense rainfall, produce low-flow responses with high surface runoff contribution, high suspended sediment concentration, and exhibit anticlockwise flow concentration hysteresis loops. This suggests that high amounts of fine sediments are mobilized on hillslopes during these floods, leading to high suspended sediment concentrations and moderate flow rates in the river network, associated with sediment deposition. Conversely, autumn/winter floods, governed by prolonged low-intensity rainfall, and characterized by enhanced groundwater contributions, produce hig

papers.title: Hydraulic behavior and solute redistribution of saline-alkali black soil: Implications for stormwater source control
papers.summary: Study Region Daqing, northeastern China, has saline-alkali soils, strong evaporation, and shallow groundwater that constrain infiltration-based stormwater source control. Study Focus We examined hydraulic behavior and water and solute redistribution in black soil amended with 0, 0.5, and 2.0% Na 2 CO 3 . Saturated hydraulic conductivity ( K s ) was measured after 0~4 wetting-drying cycles. Soil water retention was determined by the filter paper method, and unsaturated hydraulic conductivity ( K u ) was estimated with the van Genuchten-Mualem model. A complementary column experiment applied sequential rainfall depths of 10, 20, 40, and 70 mm to track soil moisture, electrical conductivity (EC), and gravel layer water EC. New Hydrological Insights for the Region: Na 2 CO 3 addition reduced initial Kₛ from 3.31 × 10 −6 m/s at 0% to 2.49 × 10 −7 and 3.02 × 10 −8 m/s at 0.5% and 2.0%. Wetting-drying caused further declines, while estimated Kᵤ remained lower in Na 2 CO 3 -amended soils over most of the modeled suction range. During sequential rainfall, the 2.0% treatment accumulated more water near the surface and responded more slowly at depth. EC decreased in the upper 20 cm but increased at 20~40 cm, while gravel layer water EC increased by only 8.9%. Low hydraulic conductivity therefore restricted vertical water transmission and promoted solute accumulation within the soil profile.

papers.title: Eco-Compatible Stabilization of Loess Mine Slopes Using a PDADMAC-Based Polymer–Mineral Composite: Hydraulic, Mechanical, and Ecological Performance
papers.summary: Rainfall-induced surface erosion of aeolian loess slopes in open-pit coal mines threatens slope stability and ecological reclamation, whereas conventional rigid protection and ordinary soil stabilizers can hardly reconcile soil reinforcement, impermeabilization, and vegetation compatibility. Here, poly(diallyldimethylammonium chloride) (PDADMAC) was compounded with nano-SiO2, carboxymethyl cellulose, sodium bentonite, and sodium lignosulfonate into a modified PDADMAC-based composite (MPDC). An L18(37) orthogonal array optimized the mix proportion (0.80, 0.50, 0.15, 1.60, and 0.10 wt.% of dry soil for PDADMAC, nano-SiO2, CMC, bentonite, and lignosulfonate, respectively), which was evaluated by shear and permeability tests, scanning electron microscopy, a 480 min rainfall test on a 38° slope model, and six-month field monitoring. The optimum mixture raised cohesion from 18.5 to 41.8 kPa and the friction angle from 26.8° to 32.7°, and cut saturated hydraulic conductivity by 74.3%. Under 480 min of rainfall, sediment loss and erosion ratio were 142.3 g m−2 and 4.7%, i.e., 88.7% and 88.8% below untreated loess, and cumulative infiltration fell by 85.4%. After six months, the treated 0–5 cm layer retained 46.6 kPa cohesion and a 2.2% fissure ratio (versus 20.8%); after 48 h of scouring, soil loss and sliding area were only 5.3 kg m−2 and 1.5 m2 per 100 m2, with Medicago sativa survival above 91.3%. MPDC thus couples soil reinforcement, seepage control, and ecological restoration.

papers.title: Study on the degradation mechanism of petroglyph carrier surfaces in Baiyin: Under water-temperature-salt coupling effects
papers.summary: The Baiyin petroglyph cluster in Gansu, China, stands as a significant piece of evidence for early human cultural exchange, showcasing distinct regional cultural traits and anthropological art value. However, the sandstone carrier of the petroglyphs has formed a composite degradation pattern characterized by crack development, void formation, and flaking peeling due to the freeze-thaw and chemical coupling weathering, driven by thermodynamic cycles and aqueous chemical processes, leading to the preservation crisis of some petroglyphs. Based on selected environmental characteristics relevant to the Baiyin petroglyph sites, laboratory freeze–thaw tests were conducted with controlled top-down infiltration of water or salt solutions to represent episodic precipitation/snowmelt infiltration and subsequent lateral moisture migration along exposed sandstone surfaces. Mass, hardness, and P-wave velocity were measured at 5-cycle intervals, while surface morphology, pore characteristics, microstructure, mineralogy, and chemical composition were characterized at 10-cycle intervals. The results show that freeze–thaw cycling progressively deteriorated the physical properties and pore structure of the sandstone, while the degradation response varied markedly with solution chemistry. Na 2 SO 4 produced the strongest macroscopic and pore-structural deterioration, whereas (NH 4 ) 2 SO 4 caused faster mineralogical changes, indicating that salt type controls not only the magnitude of deterioration but also the dominant surface-degradation pathway. A surface-porosity-based damage model was further used to quantify the damage evolution under the tested conditions.

papers.title: Experimental Investigation of Pervious-Impervious Concrete Layered System for Airport Runway Drainage
papers.source: International Journal for Research in Applied Science and Engineering Technology
papers.summary: Severe operational hazards, including dynamic hydroplaning and reduced visibility is caused by the accumulation of surface water on airfield pavements, while it also places significant strain on conventional airport drainage infrastructure. This research presents an experimental investigation into the use of pervious concrete as a Sustainable Drainage System for pavements of airport. Pervious concrete creates an interconnected microporous network that facilitates rapid surface runoff infiltration by intentionally reducing and omitting the fine aggregates. As the mechanical strength of Conventional Pavement Quality concrete is higher so its application in aviation environment is traditionally limited. This study evaluates the structural and hydraulic performance of various pervious concrete mix proportion by varying water-cement ratio, aggregate sizes and aggregate to cement ratio. Laboratory tests such as compressive strength and hydraulic conductivity are conducted at 7-day and 28-day curing interval. The primary goal is to optimize the mix design to get a viable balance between drainage performance and structural load-bearing capacity to ultimately determine the feasibility of deploying pervious concrete in specific airfield zones such as runway shoulders, taxiway edges and apron margins. Building upon these structural and hydraulic assessments, the research explores the broader operational impacts of replacing traditional impermeable surfaces. By preventing water pooling, the optimized porous matrix serves as an active safety intervention, preserving friction to the pavement and drastically cutting down aquaplaning risks during heavy rainfall. Additionally, adopting this decentralized storm water related pollutants such as unburnt hydrocarbons and heavy metal runoffs before infiltrate local water tables. The void open structure also helps to dissipate absorbed solar radiation, mitigating the localized heat Iceland effect commonly associated with massive tarmac ex

papers.title: The Invisible Depletion: Compound Drought, Groundwater Collapse, and Maladaptation in the Middle East and Southwest Asia
papers.summary: The Middle East and Southwest Asia (MESWA) region is experiencing severe hydro-climatic non-stationarity, transitioning from cyclical precipitation deficits and surpluses to a state of structural water bankruptcy. This review synthesizes the compounding atmospheric and anthropogenic drivers of this crisis, highlighting the region’s shift towards a regime defined by frequent, concurrent extremes of drought and heat ("Hot Drought" regime). While fundamental ocean-basin teleconnections (e.g., El Niño Southern Oscillation) to MESWA remain intact, their hydrological impacts have become asymmetric, with the impact of drought-causing La Niña events remaining robust even while the wetter-than-normal conditions associated with El Niño have become less reliable. This asymmetry has emerged because (1) expected moisture delivery to MESWA has been frequently deflected by persistent atmospheric blocking and (2) escalating temperatures and extreme evaporative demand have reduced snow water storage and the ability of precipitation events to recharge surface moisture and water resources. To compensate for these losses in surface water availability, the region has increasingly relied on unregulated groundwater extraction. This dynamic has created a Water-Energy-Food-Ecosystems (WEFE) maladaptation trap where governments are forced to liquidate future aquifer reserves to prevent immediate food system collapse. This anthropogenic depletion, combined with the ongoing cryospheric buffer failure, has pushed regional basins past thresholds of historical elasticity—manifesting as irreversible physical degradation such as land subsidence, and coastal salinization—locking the corridor into a state where climatic variability alone is no longer sufficient to recharge water resources. We argue that operational Early Warning Systems (EWS) must expand beyond traditional, precipitation-centric meteorological forecasting by additionally tracking absolute systemic limits using Terrestrial Water Stora

papers.title: A study on surface runoff prediction in Guangzhou using the SCS-CN model
papers.source: International Conference on Advances in Energy and Environmental Engineering (AEEE)
papers.summary: With the acceleration of urbanization, the impervious surface area in Guangzhou has expanded, leading to an increase in surface runoff and a rising frequency of urban waterlogging events. This study established localized CN parameters for Guangzhou based on the SCS-CN model, fitted rainfall amounts for different return periods, simulated surface runoff, and conducted sensitivity analysis and uncertainty quantification. The simulation results were then spatially correlated with waterlogging risk hotspots. The results show that under low return periods, risks are concentrated in low-lying areas of built-up zones, while under high return periods, risks rapidly spread to surrounding areas and the northern region, with waterlogging evolving from point-scale ponding to regional inundation. This study can provide scientific support for urban flood drainage planning and waterlogging risk early warning.

papers.title: Assessing soil erosion in understory-eroded forestlands based on the three-dimensional index of stratified vegetation volume
papers.source: Frontiers in Forests and Global Change
papers.summary: Introduction Traditional vegetation indicators such as fractional vegetation cover (FVC) and NDVI capture only horizontal extent and fail to distinguish the erosion–reduction functions of canopy, understory, and litter layers, often overestimating soil conservation in forests with closed canopies but degraded near‑surface vegetation. Methods We developed an empirical model to assess the soil erosion index (SEI) based on Stratified Vegetation Volume (cover × leaf area index or litter depth) across three vertical layers. SEI was measured from 17 standard runoff plots in a typical red soil erosion area of southern China and extrapolated to 46 natural forestland sites using a two‑variable empirical model based on bulk density and gravel content (cumulative grade accuracy: 91.1% within ± 1 erosion grade). Results Using extrapolated SEI as dependent variable and vegetation volumes of the three layers as independent variables, the three‑variable regression model performed best ( R 2 = 0.650, RMSE = 0.104). Regression coefficients followed a clear hierarchy: understory (−0.186) > litter (−0.046) > canopy (−0.040), indicating that understory vegetation contributed approximately 4.6 times more to erosion reduction than the canopy. The two‑indicator model (understory + litter) achieved the same grade classification accuracy (96.3%) as the three‑indicator model, offering a simplified pathway for rapid assessment when resources are limited. Discussion These results establish near‑surface vegetation as the core functional layer for forest soil conservation and provide a quantitative tool for diagnosing forest soil health and guiding restoration prioritization in degraded subtropical forests.

papers.title: Synergistic valorization of oil palm empty fruit bunch and pome sludge for balanced erosion control and runoff quality
papers.summary: The palm oil sector confronts significant sustainability challenges due to massive biomass waste generation, particularly Oil Palm Empty Fruit Bunches (OPEFB) and Palm Oil Mill Effluent (POME). This study aimed to valorize OPEFB-POME materials into biodegradable soil pellets in three distinct ratios to determine the optimum sludge ratio and evaluate their efficacy in mitigating soil erosion, surface runoff quality, and environmental sustainability. Rainfall simulation experiments were conducted on loamy sand, utilizing standardized soil characterization within erosion control plots at five application rates (T1, T2, T3, T4, and T5 g/ft 2 ) to evaluate the balance between physical protection and runoff quality. The results revealed that Pellet II (40:60 OPEFB-to-sludge ratio) exhibited the optimal dimensional stability, while application rate T2 provided the best balance between erosion control and runoff quality. Despite maximal pellet coverage (T5) decreasing turbidity by 97.80%, it exceeded the environmental thresholds for chemical oxygen demand (192 mg/L) and phosphorus (4.59 mg/L). Despite this rate reducing the nutrient load relative to higher application rates, it still introduced phosphorus levels exceeding eutrophication thresholds, marking it as a best-compromise solution rather than a completely benign intervention and providing the highest degree of balanced performance between physical protection and chemical runoff loading. This study highlights that OPEFB-POME pellets reflect an effective by-product valorization pathway, providing an integrated option for enhancing resource recovery in the palm oil sector by balancing soil conservation with aquatic environmental protection.

papers.title: Furrow irrigation spacing effects on water movement in a vertisol: A case study of wide‐skip furrow irrigation
papers.summary: Abstract Vertisols, also known as cracking clay soils when dry, can be prone to excessive infiltration from every‐furrow irrigation. To mitigate this problem, some farmers in the Yazoo‐Mississippi Delta practice wide‐skip furrow irrigation, which concentrates irrigation water into one furrow every 3 m or wider. How this spacing of irrigated furrows affects water movement in a vertisol was investigated through monitoring an irrigation event during an experiment with four spacing treatments: 1 m (0.25 L s −1 in every furrow), 2 m (0.51 L s −1 in every other furrow), 4 m (0.98 L s −1 in every fourth furrow), and 8 m (2.13 L s −1 in every eighth furrow). Furrow advance was similar between the 1‐m and 2‐m treatments but was 34% and 122% faster for the 4‐m and 8‐m treatments, respectively. In the 8‐m treatment, the time when wetting began was not significantly different among depths deeper than 0.3 m nor among distances 0.5–3.5 m perpendicularly away from the irrigated furrow. Such rapid vertical and lateral spread was attributed to gravity‐driven preferential flow through soil cracks. At depths shallower than 0.3 m in the 8‐m treatment, however, distances beyond 2 m from the irrigated furrow experienced delayed start of wetting, slower wetting rates, and smaller soil water increases. This trend was the principal cause of 32% less infiltration in the 8‐m treatment than in the 1‐m treatment. By characterizing the hydrological performance of wide‐skip furrow irrigation on vertisols, these findings will guide users in managing this practice to optimize the benefits and risks of purposefully nonuniform wetting.

papers.title: Living Landscapes for Restoring the Soil-Sponge Continuum: Functional Farming Systems for Drought and Flood Resilience
papers.summary: The soil-sponge continuum describes the living interaction among plants, soil structure, water, carbon, and biological activity that governs infiltration, storage, and release of soil moisture. When functioning effectively, this continuum buffers hydrological extremes by absorbing rainfall, retaining water within organic-rich and biologically active soils, and sustaining plant growth, biodiversity, and groundwater recharge. However, decades of extractive, input-intensive agriculture have weakened this capacity through soil compaction, organic carbon loss, disrupted soil biology, and simplified land use, resulting in increased runoff, soil erosion, and heightened vulnerability to both droughts and floods. This chapter presents a functional farming framework rooted in agroecology and regenerative land management for restoring the soil-sponge continuum at farm and landscape scales. Drawing on multi-scale evidence, it integrates field-based observations and living landscape models that combine multipurpose trees, crops, livestock, and people. It demonstrates how agroecosystems-driven agriculture, adaptive natural farming, and nandi-krishi restore soil biology, health and strengthen root-zone water-holding capacity, and enhance green water flow. By explicitly linking soil biology, hydrological processes, and carbon dynamics, this chapter shows that functional farming systems can stabilize productivity, enhance biodiversity, reduce input costs, and transform agricultural landscapes into drought- and flood-resilient systems. It concludes by outlining scalable pathways for soil-sponge restoration through individual farmers to community collective actions, satellite and AI-enabled soil-moisture intelligence, and integrated policy and planning approaches, positioning living landscapes as a cornerstone of climate-resilient and regenerative agriculture.

papers.title: Integrating surface-active layer-permafrost hydrological processes: A systematic review and research framework
papers.summary: Abstract. Climate warming has accelerated permafrost degradation, leading to significant challenges in water circulation and transformation. Since the early 21st century, especially during the last ten years, permafrost hydrology has garnered substantial attention, yielding a wealth of research outcomes. However, a comprehensive and systematic understanding of the permafrost hydrology remains limited. This study synthesised the current knowledge through an extensive literature review and systematic analysis, establishing a foundational framework for permafrost hydrology. The framework integrated three critical dimensions: surface hydrological processes, hydrological functions of the active layer, and the hydrological effects of permafrost changes. Subsequently, the current state, trends, and challenges in permafrost hydrology research were summarised, and a holistic overview was provided. Regarding surface hydrological processes in permafrost regions, this study examined the impacts of freeze-thaw cycles on surface runoff from multiple perspectives, including the influence of active layer thawing, slope hydrological processes, river channel dynamics, large-scale permafrost hydrology, and the hydrological consequences of thermokarst formation. For hydrological processes within the active layer, the study identified the hydrological role of the active layer, key factors influencing its hydrological behaviour, and the interactions between suprapermafrost water and soil water. Concerning the hydrological impacts of permafrost thaw, this study investigated the transformation dynamics between surface and groundwater in permafrost regions by analysing the effects of climate change through increased baseflow, groundwater recharge, and subsurface runoff. Finally, this study outlined future research directions, emphasising three key areas: the application of novel observational methods, integrated surface-subsurface investigations, and the ecological and environmental impacts

papers.title: Enhancing urban water resilience through green infrastructure in Kathmandu, Nepal
papers.summary: Rapidly growing cities in developing countries, including Kathmandu, Nepal, are struggling to handle water issues driven by both urban growth and climate change. Conventional grey infrastructure is unable to address the rising problems of flooding, polluted water, and declining groundwater recharge. This work evaluates how Green Infrastructure (GI) might help make Kathmandu Valley more sustainable and enhance ecosystem resilience through better water management. This study develops an integrated urban water resilience framework for Kathmandu Valley by combining geospatial analysis, hydrological modelling, field-based assessment of GI interventions, and stakeholder-driven policy evaluation. The interdisciplinary approach enables simultaneous examination of environmental performance, spatial vulnerability, and institutional implementation challenges associated with GI adoption in a rapidly urbanising Himalayan city. GI interventions reduced surface runoff by up to 40%, improved water quality by reducing nutrient loads (BOD, nitrate, phosphate) by over 60%, and mitigated urban heat by 3–4 °C. Spatial analysis identified priority zones for GI implementation along the Bagmati River corridor and in low-lying urban areas of Kathmandu Valley. Stakeholders expressed strong public support for GI initiatives but highlighted weak institutional coordination and limited maintenance capacity as major implementation challenges. This research helps build evidence for ecological adaptation and suggests useful steps to make Kathmandu’s infrastructure more resilient, livable, and ecologically adaptive.

papers.title: Landslide‐Channel Coupling Controls Asymmetric Flash Flood—Debris Flow Transitions: Insights From an Extreme Rainfall‐Induced Hazard Chain in Yuzhong of China in 2025
papers.summary: Abstract Extreme rainfall‐triggered landslide–flash flood–debris flow hazard chains (LFFDF) are increasingly responsible for hydroclimatic losses worldwide. Although dynamics of individual hazards are established, transition mechanisms within LFFDF governed by coupled landslide–channel responses remain unresolved. Taking a catastrophic LFFDF event in northwestern China in 2025, we reconstructed the transition dynamics of the hazard chain using satellite data, seismic records, and numerical modeling. The results show that the LFFDF cascade operates as asymmetric transition processes, in which the dominant controls are state‐dependent. Rainfall‐induced landslides supplied one‐third of the mobilized sediment; their interaction with flash floods increased channel‐flow Shields stress by more than an order of magnitude, prematurely initiating debris flows in headwater channels. The downstream reversion from debris flow to flash flood is mainly controlled by the thickness and saturation state of channel sediments. Finally, we suggest a cascade‐based paradigm for risk assessment to enhance community resilience to LFFDF risks.

papers.title: A multi-source quantitative reconstruction of the 26 August 2026 Bhote Koshi rock-ice avalanche-debris-flow-flood cascade, Nepal
papers.summary: On 26 August 2026, a catastrophic transboundary mass-flow and flood cascade originated in the upper Lhende Khola-Bhote Koshi headwaters and propagated through the Bhote Koshi, Trishuli, and Narayani river system in Nepal. Early public descriptions used the glacial lake outburst flood (GLOF) label, but subsequent seismic, satellite, video, field, hydrological, and damage-assessment evidence supported a more complex sequence of rock-ice avalanche, progressive entrainment and debris-flow transformation, followed by downstream flood-wave routing. This study aims to provide a reproducible, evidence-weighted quantitative reconstruction using publicly available data through 7 October 2026. Official hydrometeorological timelines, peer-reviewed source-process studies, preliminary satellite mapping, the Government of Nepal Rapid Damage and Needs Assessment, and dated human-impact snapshots were harmonized. Propagation and warning-time metrics, hydrological amplification, paired channel-width change at 22 sections, exposure and infrastructure severity ratios, and sectoral concentration of disaster effects and recovery needs were calculated. The source-to-border segment was reported at approximately 188 km/h (52.2 m/s), declining to 23-26 km/h in lower-river segments which was explained by a descriptive log-linear decay model at 80.1% of variation across six reported segment speeds. The public-warning anchor at 09:15 Nepal Standard Time occurred 38 minutes after the source seismic signal, after the flood had already passed or disabled upper-corridor stations, leaving only five minutes to the Betrawati station-failure proxy but 365 minutes to the reported Devghat flood-wave arrival. At Devghat, stage rose from 4.76 to 6.57 m, and discharge increased from approximately 2,600 to 5,850 m3/s where the reported 19.96 million m3 excess volume represented 34.8% of total flow volume during 14:10-18:00. All 22 mapped channel sections widened, from a mean of 66.1 to 266.5 m with the mean

papers.title: Reducing the Footprint of Agriculture Through Sustainable Land Management Practices
papers.source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.summary: Soil degradation and desertification represent major challenges for Mediterranean ecosystems. Unsustainable land management practices have altered vegetation structure and density, accelerating soil erosion and desertification processes. In response, many Mediterranean regions have adopted sustainable land management strategies, reducing human pressure such as agriculture's footprint. Here we present and five cases around the Mediterranean where such strategies have been implemented instead of unsustainable ones and we highlight their outcomes. Ιn Stornara and Tara, Puglia, Italy, where aquifer irrigation and unlicensed wells are widely used, worsening groundwater depletion and salinisation. Through organic farming practices in table grape production, soil organic matter is increased, enhancing water retention. Integrating native species into the farming system increases resilience for pests and diseases. At the same time, biodiversity conservation within agricultural production is also retained as cover crops are used as well. In Tamia, Fayoum, Egypt Integrated soil fertility management, improved plant varieties, water diversion and drainage. The area is under pressure because of degraded soil and water quality. More specifically, the area of Tamia is characterised by salt-affected soils whilst also being calcareous – containing over 10% calcium carbonate. To tackle these, several strategies have been implemented including salt-tolerant species and varieties have been selected, application of organic and bio fertilizers, mulching, and subsurface drainage system. By the implementing these, enhanced crop performance, improved soil structure and organic content, improved water retention and drought resistance and better water quality is achieved. In Spain at the outskirts of Valencia, they face soil erosion coupled with reduced precipitation. papers.title: Unsaturated Soil Behavior Under Repeated Traffic Loading in Arid Climates: A Scenario-Based Numerical Study of Road Subgrade Performance Under Assumed Climate-Analogue Suction Pathways
papers.summary: Road subgrade response in arid regions is governed by the unsaturated state of the soil, yet pavement design frameworks represent moisture mainly through empirical, largely equilibrium environmental adjustments rather than through the explicit evolution of matric suction during wetting and drying. Climate influence is represented by a two-suction concept that separates the annual-average drying trend from the critical post-rainfall wetted state. The suction pathways are not derived from Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 6 (CMIP6) output: their end-of-life values (140 and 55 kPa) are prescribed, and they are labelled Shared Socioeconomic Pathway (SSP) SSP2-4.5 and SSP5-8.5 analogues only because their direction and ordering are qualitatively consistent with the projections of the Sixth Assessment Report (AR6) of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) for arid regions. They are treated throughout as assumed scenario parameters. All soil, traffic and deformation parameters are representative literature-based values; no measured retention, resilient modulus or rutting data are used, so every result is a conditional model output and not a validated prediction. Under the assumed high-emission analogue the computed year-20 subgrade rut depth is 22.0 mm (parameter-perturbation range 12-31 mm), reaching the 20 mm rut-depth threshold adopted here between years 19 and 20, against 6.5 mm for the constant-climate baseline and 11.1 mm for the moderate analogue. A one-at-a-time sensitivity screening ranks the assumed pathway shift (+15.5 mm) first, followed by design suction (+4.6/-1.8 mm), the initial-strain (ε0) scaling and the exponent β, with traffic growth least influential.

papers.title: Multivariate analysis of compound hydroclimatic extremes in snow-fed sub-catchments: an application for climate-resilient water management of Narayani Basin, Nepal
papers.summary: Compound hydroclimatic extremes challenge water management worldwide due to their complex and nonlinear hydrological impacts. Drought-to-flood (DtF) events occur when prolonged dry periods are followed by rapid wet anomalies with distinct impacts from regular floods. Such events occur across diverse hydroclimatic settings; in heterogeneous snow-fed basins, DtF behaviour is governed by precipitation variability, antecedent soil-moisture conditions, snow processes, and, where present, reservoir regulation. This study investigates DtF transitions across six sub-catchments of the Narayani River Basin, Nepal, using monthly precipitation (17 stations), streamflow (6 gauges), remote sensing soil moisture, and historical drought–flood records. Historical DtF events were fitted with monthly Standardized Precipitation Index (SPI) signals, and sensitivity analysis of three ΔSPI thresholds (1.0, 1.25, and 1.5) identified 1.25 as the optimal criterion for distinguishing meaningful DtF transitions. The calibrated ΔSPI framework identifies DtF events and integrates ΔSPI–ΔSSI regression with multivariate Principal Component Analysis (PCA) of ΔSPI, ΔSSI, and ΔSWDI to investigate coupled hydroclimatic controls and process-level DtF dynamics. Results reveal pronounced spatial contrasts across hydroclimatic regimes. Highly snow-dominated Budhi Gandaki exhibits weak or opposing ΔSPI–ΔSSI responses during snow storage, followed by strengthened rainfall–runoff coupling during snowmelt (R2 up to 0.96). Moderately snow-influenced sub- catchments display mixed rainfall–runoff responses (R2 = 0.02–0.79), reflecting varying contributions of snowmelt and rainfall, whereas rainfed reservoir- regulated Tadi Khola and Rapti show weak pre-monsoon responses during reservoir filling (R2 = 0.001–0.96) and shift to strong monsoon coupling (R2 = 0.75–1.00) during reservoir release. PCA shows that PC1 explains 40%–100% of the joint ΔSPI–ΔSSI–ΔSWDI variance, with contrasting loading directions between pre

papers.title: Scalable and locally mass-conservative simulation of basin-scale variably saturated groundwater flow
papers.summary: Groundwater is the largest store of liquid fresh water, yet because it is hidden beneath the surface, it is primarily understood through models of porous-media flow. Richards' equation, a physically faithful description of variably saturated groundwater flow, remains costly for basin-scale groundwater modelling. Consequently, operational models use reduced physics, either by assuming linearity or by using approximate solutions. Here, we introduce a scalable, open-source, three-dimensional solver for variably saturated groundwater flow implemented in G-ADOPT, an automated finite-element platform built on Firedrake. The implementation combines a locally conservative discontinuous Galerkin discretisation, Newton iteration with an exact Jacobian, implicit time integration through the Irksome library, used here with Backward Euler, and vertically lumped multigrid preconditioners designed for the extreme aspect ratios of production scenarios. We verify accuracy, convergence, and strict local mass conservation on two- and three-dimensional benchmarks, and apply the solver to the Lower Murrumbidgee floodplain in New South Wales, Australia. The model covers approximately 30 000 km^2, contains several hundred million degrees of freedom, and uses public stratigraphic, rainfall, and water-table data. Our scaling experiments show that the effectiveness of the preconditioner is controlled primarily by the physical regime in which the model is integrated. A single-level method (e.g., block-Jacobi ILU(0)) suffices at the short time steps of an infiltration study, but at seasonal time steps, the admissible time step decreases significantly under horizontal refinement. In a near-saturated profile without specific storage, such single-level methods do not converge at any tested step size. By contrast, a vertically lumped coarse-space preconditioner takes the full three-month step on every mesh, requiring four to ten linear iterations per Newton step and reducing wall-clock time by a f

papers.title: FLOWS: a model to simulate water and solutes fluxes in agricultural and environmental systems. 1. Theory and applications with intercode benchmarking
papers.summary: Abstract FLOWS (FLOws of Water and Solutes in soils) is a dynamic physically-based model to simulate water flow and solute transport in the soil–plant–atmosphere system. The numerical code was written in MATLAB. One-dimensional vertical transient water flow is simulated by numerically solving the 1D form of the Richards equation (RE) using an implicit, backward, finite differences scheme with explicit linearization. As for the solutes, the code solves the 1D Advection Dispersion equation (ADE) by an explicit, central difference scheme, allowing for a relatively easy inclusion of non-linear adsorption and other non-linear processes. The model produces information on the time evolution of (among many other outputs): soil water contents and pressure potentials in the soil profile; solute (tracers, adsorbed, volatile and reactive solutes) concentrations in the soil profile; water and solute uptake and actual evapotranspiration for simulated crops; deep percolation water and solute fluxes; root uptake of water and solutes, also in presence of water and osmotic stresses; water fluxes and related solute fluxes to runoff; drainage water fluxes and related solute fluxes; irrigation fluxes computed by the model; and temperature in the soil profile. Compared to other existing models, some specificities of FLOWS model are: (1) integrated simulation of carbon, nitrogen and phosphorus transformations and transport contextually to the simulation of water contents and fluxes; (2) macroscopic root uptake; (3) irrigation management, by allowing to optimize the time scheduling and volumes according to some criterion based on the average pressure head in the root zone; (4) the possibility of running multi-site simulations, which may be especially important for spatially distributed simulations; and (5) an interactive graphical user interface, allowing the user to easily handle even large input files and seeing the simulation results by graphical display of the main output variables.

papers.title: Rainfall partitioning and contrasting local understory runoff and soil loss responses among three vegetation communities in a karst restoration area
papers.summary: Study region Puding County, southwestern China, a karst area characterized by severe rocky desertification and long-term ecological restoration. Study focus Vegetation restoration alters canopy structure and rainfall redistribution, but how these changes relate to localized understory runoff and soil loss remains unclear. We monitored 31 rainfall events in three vegetation communities dominated by Platycladus orientalis , Platycarya strobilacea , and Viburnum dilatatum . Community-scale throughfall, stemflow, and canopy interception were quantified, while runoff and soil loss were monitored in subcanopy and stem-base microplots. Mixed-effects models were used to assess rainfall, microsite, and environmental associations. New hydrological insights for the region Throughfall was the largest rainfall-partitioning component and was highest in P. orientalis (86.21%), although this community did not show the strongest erosion response. P. strobilacea had the greatest runoff and soil loss, with mean soil loss of 28.97 and 61.79 g m⁻² in subcanopy and stem-base microsites, respectively. Gross rainfall showed strong nonlinear associations with runoff and soil loss. Slope and bare-soil cover were positively associated with both responses, whereas saturated hydraulic conductivity was negatively associated. After accounting for gross rainfall, community-level throughfall fraction provided no significant additional explanatory information for subcanopy runoff or soil loss. Because stemflow to individual stem-base microplots was not directly measured, stem-base responses were interpreted as integrated microsite responses.

papers.title: Evaluating multi-benefit strip-cropping systems for climate-resilient agricultural landscapes in Malawi
papers.source: CGSPace A Repository of Agricultural Research Outputs (Consultative Group for International Agricultural Research)
papers.summary: Soil erosion, land degradation, and declining soil fertility continue to threaten agricultural productivity and food security across Malawi, particularly in sloping landscapes where runoff and soil loss are prevalent. These challenges are expected to intensify under climate change due to increasing rainfall variability and more frequent extreme weather events. While various soil and water conservation technologies have been promoted, their adoption by smallholder farmers has often been constrained by labor requirements, land-use trade-offs, and limited short-term economic benefits. Consequently, there is growing interest in integrated farming approaches that simultaneously enhance productivity, improve resilience, and conserve natural resources. This study evaluated the performance of strip-cropping systems as a strategy for developing resilient agricultural landscapes in Malawi. The approach integrates contour-aligned grass strips with maize and legumes within productive farmland to reduce runoff and erosion while maintaining crop production and generating livestock feed. The study aimed to assess the agronomic, fodder, and conservation potential of alternative strip-cropping configurations across contrasting slope conditions and to identify systems capable of balancing productivity and sustainability objectives. Field experiments were established on farmer-managed fields representing gentle (5–15%) and steep (15–25%) slope categories. Four cropping systems were evaluated using a randomized complete block design with three replications per farm: (i) Grass–Maize–Grass (GMG), (ii) Grass–Maize–Grass–Maize–Grass (GMGMG), (iii) Grass–Maize–Legume–Maize–Grass (GMLMG), and (iv) a maize monocrop control. Mixed-effects models were used to assess treatment effects while accounting for farmer-to-farmer variability. Results showed that cropping system significantly influenced maize grain yield and overall system productivity, whereas slope category and treatment × slope intera

papers.title: INOVASI GUDACELL (GRATING U-DITCH AND AQUACELL) SEBAGAI SISTEM DRAINASE TERINTEGRASI UNTUK MENDUKUNG PENGENDALIAN GENANGAN DI JALAN SULUH, KELURAHAN SIDOREJO HILIR, KECAMATAN MEDAN TEMBUNG, KOTA MEDAN
papers.source: Didaktik Jurnal Ilmiah PGSD STKIP Subang
papers.summary: Urban inundation is often associated with limited drainage capacity, waste accumulation, sedimentation, and reduced infiltration areas. Field observations reported in the source document identified these issues along Jalan Suluh, Sidorejo Hilir, Medan Tembung, Medan, where inundation during heavy rainfall was reported to reach approximately 30–40 cm. This article describes GUDACELL (Grating U-Ditch AquaCell), a proposed local drainage-support system that integrates a waste-screening grating, a U-Ditch conveyance channel, and an AquaCell temporary storage unit. The study uses a descriptive design-development approach based on field observation, literature review, concept adaptation, and product planning. The proposed operating sequence is “screen, convey, store, and infiltrate”: the grating intercepts certain solid waste, the U-Ditch directs runoff, and the AquaCell temporarily stores water before infiltration or controlled discharge. The literature reviewed in the source document supports sustainable drainage approaches that combine conveyance, temporary storage, and infiltration rather than relying solely on conventional channels. However, the available material does not provide controlled prototype-test results or measured reductions in flood depth. Therefore, GUDACELL should be regarded as a proposed supporting innovation whose hydraulic capacity, infiltration performance, structural durability, and maintenance requirements need to be verified through further testing and site-specific design.

papers.title: Bridging nature-based solutions, smart technologies, and traditional wisdom for sustainable water management: a multi-decadal evaluation of bamboo-based systems in degraded ravine landscapes
papers.summary: ABSTRACT Nature-based Solutions (NbS) are increasingly recognized as sustainable approaches for addressing water insecurity, land degradation, biodiversity loss, and climate resilience. However, robust long-term field evidence quantifying their hydrological and ecological effectiveness remains limited. This study presents a multi-decadal (1985–2025) evidence synthesis evaluating bamboo-based NbS for restoring degraded ravine landscapes in India by integrating long-term field observations, experimental watershed investigations, hydrological monitoring, project datasets, and peer-reviewed literature. Results demonstrate that bamboo functions as living hydrological infrastructure by enhancing rainfall retention, increasing infiltration, reducing runoff and sediment transport, improving soil quality, and accelerating ecological recovery. Bamboo-based interventions reduced runoff by 80–90%, soil loss by 85–95%, and sediment yield by over 90%, while stabilizing gullies within 2–3 years. Infiltration increased substantially (up to ∼140 cm h−1) together with improvements in soil organic carbon and micro-ecological conditions. Economically, bamboo systems generated annual returns of ₹33,500–48,000 ha−1 with internal rates of return of 18–22%. The study proposes an integrated Nature-Based Hydrological Engineering framework, establishing bamboo as a scalable, climate-resilient solution for watershed restoration, erosion control, and sustainable water management in degraded landscapes worldwide.

papers.title: Stable water isotopes as critical constraints for ecohydrological flux partitioning in a West African basin
papers.summary: Abstract. This study investigates the added value of stable water isotopes in constraining ecohydrological flux partitioning within the Bétérou basin, a 10,000 km² tropical savanna watershed in northern Benin. It leverages a unique five-year record of high-frequency isotope measurements in river water at the outlet and in precipitation. Using the tracer-enabled, distributed model EcH2O-iso, we evaluated how different calibration datasets influence the representation of internal flux partitioning, in particular runoff generation from surface and subsurface pathways, in a region where evapotranspiration (ET) dominates the water budget. A multi-objective calibration was performed across four scenarios, ranging from a baseline using only outlet discharge to a comprehensive setup incorporating intra-basin discharge and isotopic tracers. Our results demonstrate that isotopic tracers are essential for realistically reproducing internal flow partitioning. The inclusion of isotopes drove the model to mobilise older groundwater reservoirs, leading to increased simulated water ages and the dampening of stream isotopic signals. Scenarios calibrated solely on outlet discharge showed high fit for the hydrograph but simulated minimal subsurface contribution, contrary to field evidence from instrumented catchments. Isotopes provided only indirect constraints on ET, whose influence on water partitioning was governed primarily by root water uptake as modulated by land cover. These findings suggest that monitoring strategies in tropical environments where data are often scarce and monitoring priorities must be carefully weighed, should consider the inclusion of isotopic tracers alongside traditional hydrometric observations, as these constrain models to reproduce hydrological functioning for the right reasons and thus provide a more reliable basis for assessing water resources and climate change vulnerability.

papers.title: Temporal dynamics of hydrological impacts of adjustable weirs in an open ditch: an experiment-modeling study on a shallow groundwater environment
papers.summary: Abstract. Adjustable weirs have been used to block ditch waters especially during wet seasons to retain more shallow groundwater in agricultural fields and forests. However, to fully verify the effectiveness of weirs, quantifying the weirs’ hydrological benefits to vegetation and nearby surface waters is important. Our study quantified the hydrological impacts of these weirs on the water balance across seasons under wet and dry years. We performed field experiments in a 2% sloped parcel with a single ditch and two weirs in Merelbeke-Melle, Belgium. Then, we used a 3D subsurface flow model (HYDRUS 5) to represent the phreatic and vadose zones underlying the regional hillslope. They were calibrated using water table levels monitored across the parcel in 2022–2026, covering both wet and dry years. Afterwards, we simulated separate scenarios for empty and full ditches under shallow and deep rooting depth parameterizations. The observed water tables show little responses with opening and closing of weirs. Meanwhile, simulations involving weir management exhibited higher water tables especially closer to the ditch due to reduced field drainage that retain more water during wet periods and also infiltration of ditch waters during dry periods. Yet this boosted water availability was partitioned mainly to runoff, storage, and excess (added) field drainage downstream of the weirs. The stream downslope (Gondebeek stream) had only little additional baseflows. Moreover, the vegetation experienced both wet and drought stresses that inhibited uptake of water gained from water management. Thus, hydrological models on weir management should properly consider the presence and sources of infiltrating ditch waters, vegetation dynamics in the field, and the meteorological context (seasonality, interannual variability).

It supports the paper "Future hydrology of a Himalayan mountainous basin shaped by elevation dependent shifts in water balance components" and allows the reported results to be reproduced. All hydrological outputs come from the fully distributed SPHY model (Spatial Processes in HYdrology, version 3.0). Contents 01_static: basin DEM, basin boundary and Chisapani outlet shapefiles. 02_maps: long-term mean annual and monthly water balance maps (rainfall, snowfall, evapotranspiration, total runoff, rainfall runoff, snowmelt runoff, baseflow, infiltration, groundwater recharge and others) for the reference period (1991-2020) and for 15 future runs (mid- and late-century). 03_time_series: daily discharge (total, rainfall runoff, snowmelt, glacier melt and baseflow) for the reference period and all future runs; daily basin-average and elevation-band precipitation and temperature; wet-day counts; monthly rainfall and snowfall per 1000 m elevation band. 04_FOSM: parameter-perturbation runs (TCrit, snow degree-day factor, baseflow recession coefficient, groundwater recharge delay, crop coefficients), stored in perturbations/, and an unperturbed baseline/. Both have reference_period and future_period subfolders (future runs use SSP3-7.0). Model and scenarios Model: SPHY 3.0, daily time step, 500 m resolution. Climate forcing: five ISIMIP3b models (GFDL-ESM4, IPSL-CM6A-LR, MPI-ESM1-2-HR, MRI-ESM2-0, UKESM1-0-LL). Scenarios: SSP1-2.6, SSP3-7.0, SSP5-8.5 (15 model-scenario runs). papers.title: Field measurement of hydraulic conductivity in a compacted filtered iron ore tailings stack using mini-infiltrometer tests
papers.summary: This paper presents a field-based assessment of near-surface hydraulic conductivity in a compacted filtered iron ore tailings stack using mini-infiltrometer tests. A total of 115 in situ measurements were performed on the compacted surface, providing a dataset for evaluating the variability of near-surface field measurements under controlled suction conditions. The mini-infiltrometer results are interpreted as hydraulic conductivity values associated with the pressure head applied at the porous disk–tailings interface, not necessarily as fully saturated hydraulic conductivity. The measured values ranged from 1.14 × 10−7 m/s to 4.59 × 10−6 m/s, with an arithmetic mean of 1.31 × 10−6 m/s, a median of 1.20 × 10−6 m/s, and a geometric mean of 1.12 × 10−6 m/s. Although the results were concentrated around 10−6 m/s, the coefficient of variation was approximately 56.9%, indicating relevant relative variability. Most values were located between 5.0 × 10−7 m/s and 3.0 × 10−6 m/s, supporting the use of the geometric mean as a representative central estimate for engineering analyses. The influence of imposed suction (h0 ) was also examined; however, no systematic dependence on the applied values was identified. Comparison with published data shows that the results fall within the range reported for compacted and filtered tailings, while reinforcing that hydraulic conductivity cannot be inferred from void ratio alone. The study highlights the importance of direct field measurements for supporting seepage analyses, transient flow modelling, water balance assessments, and hydraulic characterization of filtered tailings stacks.

papers.title: Diagnosis and causal-chain-based treatment of water-leakage in in-service mountainous highway tunnels: an engineering application
papers.summary: Water leakage in in-service mountainous highway tunnels is difficult to diagnose due to concealed geological conditions, coupled seepage processes, and frequent recurrence after local repair. This study proposes a causal-diagnosis and causal-chain-based treatment framework for tunnel water leakage. The water-leakage mechanism is interpreted as a progressive process involving groundwater recharge, fracture-controlled seepage transport, drainage obstruction, water-pressure accumulation behind the lining, and failure at weak points in the waterproofing system. A diagnostic method integrating leakage characteristics, groundwater conditions, geological anomalies behind the lining, drainage performance, and waterproofing defects is established, followed by a three-stage treatment strategy. The framework was applied to the Dashiling Tunnel on the Shenzhen–Cenxi Expressway (G2518), China, using leakage surveys, seismic reflection imaging, and visual inspections. A total of 312 leakage defects were identified, with 48.1% occurring at secondary-lining construction joints and 37.8% occurring in wall-foot-to-sidewall zones. Fracture-related anomalies behind the lining and severe blockage in 50.0% of the inspected side drains revealed a compound leakage mechanism. After targeted treatment, two years of monitoring showed that the total area of pavement leakage was reduced to approximately 3.9% of its pre-treatment level. The number of tunnel water-leakage defects exhibited an approximately linear decreasing trend, with an overall reduction of more than 70%. The densities of tunnel water-leakage defects in all statistical sections were less than 0.3 points per linear meter, demonstrating good treatment effectiveness. The proposed framework provides a practical approach for the systematic diagnosis and treatment of water leakage in comparable in-service mountainous highway tunnels with similar hydrogeological and drainage conditions.

papers.title: Integrating Mean Weight Diameter and Environmental Sensitivity Index for Modeling Soil Erosion Risk and Land Degradation in Soils under Different Agricultural Land Uses
papers.source: The Eurasia Proceedings of Science Technology Engineering and Mathematics
papers.summary: The study area is located between latitudes (36°42′24.52″ N – 36°24′38.40″ N) and longitudes (43°38′14.98″ E – 43°22′14.58″ E), covering an area 1245 km². The elevation ranges from 283 to 1015 m above sea level. The climate classified as a transitional zone between semi-arid and Mediterranean climates. Twenty-five sites were selected within the study area. Approximately 2 kg of soil was collected per site, with samples carefully selected to ensure homogeneity. The samples were then transported to the laboratory, air-dried, gently crushed using a wooden hammer, and sieved through a 2 mm mesh sieve. Subsequently, they were stored in plastic containers for further physical and chemical analyses. Laboratory analyses included the determination of soil organic matter, calcium carbonate (CaCO₃) content, and particle size distribution, and Environmental Sensitivity Index equations were applied.The results indicated that the dominant soil textures in the study area ranged from clay to clay loam.. This variability is primarily attributed to differences in soil organic matter content and calcium carbonate levels, which reached maximum values of 2.28% and 37.2%, respectively. Furthermore, the results revealed relatively uniform sorting values across most sites, indicating a generally homogeneous particle size distribution, except for site, which exhibited a high sorting value of 2.420, reflecting poorer sediment uniformity. The study demonstrates that both water and wind erosion processes in the region are controlled by a complex interaction of natural and anthropogenic factors acting simultaneously, which significantly influence soil stability and susceptibility to detachment and transport.

papers.title: Land cover change and groundwater recharge at Jeju Global Education City
papers.source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.summary: Jeju Island relies heavily on groundwater recharged through its permeable volcanic terrain. This study examines how development of the Jeju Global Education City, where site construction began in 2009, changed surface infiltration and what this implies for groundwater recharge. Land-cover maps from 2007 and 2025 were compared over 378.9 ha of mapped cover within the legal planning boundary. Single-ring infiltration tests were carried out on Gotjawal, rough grass and artificial grass, with five trials per surface; one rough-grass trial did not finish within 300 s and was excluded from rate statistics. Under a scenario that treats artificial grass as non-recharging, the share of the site treated as sealed rose from 2.5% to 27.8%, an increase of approximately 95.9 ha. Every Gotjawal trial infiltrated faster than every grass trial, although the apparatus supports only a relative comparison. Applying published recharge fractions of 9 to 48% to rainfall on the newly sealed area gives a potential recharge loss of 102,000 to 545,000 m³ per year from sealing alone. These are conditional estimates rather than a measured change in aquifer recharge.

papers.title: Pore-Scale Gas Invasion and Residual Liquid Trapping in a Hydrophilic Microfluidic Network
papers.summary: Abstract Gas invasion into liquid-saturated hydrophilic porous media is governed by interfacial, wetting, viscous, and pore-scale effects that control pathway selection and residual liquid trapping. However, how liquid composition influences gas-pathway establishment, postbreakthrough redistribution, and final liquid retention remains insufficiently understood. Here, nitrogen displacement was visualized in a hydrophilic glass microfluidic network initially saturated with 12 liquid systems, including water, 3.5 wt % NaCl brine, and formulations containing ethanol, polyethylene glycol (PEG), sodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS), or sodium dodecylbenzenesulfonate (SDBS). Breakthrough time, liquid-saturation evolution, final residual liquid saturation, stabilization time, and final gas morphology were quantified. Three invasion modes were identified: preferential-channel flow, dendritic expansion, and network-like expansion. Breakthrough times ranged from 1 to 67 s, showing that rapid formation of a spanning gas pathway did not necessarily correspond to extensive liquid removal. PEG system W5 showed the highest final residual liquid saturation (∼0.42), whereas SDBS system W11 showed the lowest (∼0.07), corresponding to a final gas occupancy of ∼0.93. SDS system W8 and SDBS system W10 both exhibited high final gas occupancy together with relatively short stabilization times. Lower measured air–liquid surface tension was associated with broader branched invasion in some systems, while final liquid removal likely reflected coupled effects of viscosity, wettability, and pore-structure heterogeneity. Film-like residual liquid and locally isolated gas regions further showed that extensive gas occupation did not necessarily ensure complete connectivity among the optically resolved gas-filled regions. These results reveal a decoupling between breakthrough dynamics and final liquid removal and provide mechanistic pore-scale insight relevant to evaluating water-block mitigation in hydrat

papers.title: Comparative Assessment of Carbon Nanotube and Steel Fiber Reinforcement in Recycled Aggregate Shotcrete
papers.source: International Journal of Advanced Engineering and Technology Research
papers.summary: Recycled coarse aggregate shotcrete (RCAS) offers a resource-efficient route for underground support, but adhered mortar, heterogeneous interfaces and brittle crack propagation limit its mechanical reliability. This study critically integrates two independent experimental investigations of multi-walled carbon nanotube (MWCNT) and steel-fiber (SF) modification to evaluate the complementary roles of matrix-scale densification and crack-scale bridging. The original experimental conditions are preserved while comparable strength, deformation, pore-structure and tensile-energy indicators are examined. In the MWCNT-modified mixtures, a dosage of 0.06 wt% yielded the highest reported 28 d compressive strength (38.25 MPa), whereas 0.09 wt% maximized the splitting-tensile (3.95 MPa) and flexural (4.88 MPa) strengths. Higher dosages reduced performance as dispersion deteriorated. In the separate SF-reinforced series, increasing recycled aggregate replacement from 0% to 100% reduced direct-tensile strength from 2.6 to 2.2 MPa, whereas increasing fiber content from 0% to 2% at 50% replacement increased tensile strength from 1.5 to 3.3 MPa. Together, these observations distinguish nano-scale hydration and pore refinement from fiber-mediated stress transfer after cracking. A mechanism-based reinforcement framework is proposed to balance constructability, strength, ductility and energy absorption. Because the two experimental programs differ in aggregate quality, mixture design and test conditions, combined MWCNT–SF effects remain a hypothesis requiring dedicated experimental validation.
