papers.title: Geotechnical and Rheological Characteristics of Fine-Grained Sediments and Influencing Factors for Debris Flow Mobility
papers.summary: Fine-grained sediments that are remolded after slope failure may transform into debris flows; therefore, their post-failure mobility is better described by rheological parameters than by conventional intact-soil strength alone. This study evaluates the geotechnical and rheological behavior of natural fine-grained sediments collected in the Republic of Korea, using fall cone tests, steady-state shear tests, and oscillatory shear tests. The fall cone test was used to determine the remolded undrained shear strength, whereas the rheometer tests were used to estimate Bingham yield stress, Bingham viscosity, and dynamic yield points derived from storage and loss moduli. The results show shear-thinning behavior over the tested shear-rate range and indicate that rheological yield stresses are generally higher than the remolded undrained shear strength. In oscillatory shear, the fall cone strength lies between the first yield point, associated with the elastic or static regime, and the second yield point, associated with the onset of flow. These results suggest that undrained shear strength can be used as a simplified input when yield stress cannot be measured directly, but it should be interpreted as the maximum resistance of fully remolded soil rather than as a direct substitute for rheological yield stress.

papers.title: Impact of Climate Change on Sediment Transfer and Associated Debris Flow Management: A Case Study in the Swiss Alps
papers.summary: In recent decades, the Swiss Alps have been affected by climate change at a much higher rate than the global average. Several signs, including hydrological modifications and changes in the frequency or magnitude of slope instabilities, are altering the landscape. Rock glaciers show very high melting rates that can lead to severe debris flow events and thus a change in both the associated risk and vulnerability of the population in affected areas. This leads public authorities to constantly increase the share of their budget allocated to natural hazards in order to maintain the risk at an acceptable level. In canton Wallis (Southwestern Swiss Alps), 200 sediment retention basins have been built since 1950, representing an average annual cost of roughly 75 million Swiss francs. In this paper, we want to expose with a case study, how climate change and geomorphological modifications can affect the management of natural hazards such as debris flow. The Péterey torrent is a stream flowing from the Bonnard rock glacier above the village of Zinal, and episodes of debris flow and slope erosion put the village under pressure. Previous geomorphological analysis and recorded environmental data show an increase in glacier movements and sediment transfer through debris flow. Here in Zinal, public authorities invested 4 million Swiss francs to increase the resilience of infrastructure and mitigate the risk for the local residents. Among other measures, the retention basin capacity was increased by 700% to reach 40,000 to 60,000 m3.

papers.title: The 2026 Rasuwa Disaster: A Transboundary Rock–Ice Avalanche, Himalayan Tsunami, and Cascading Hazards
papers.summary: The Himalaya is increasingly affected by high-mountain disasters driven by the interactions among cryospheric change since 1990, slope instability, thawing of glacial deposits and rock-mass permafrost, avalanches, and river systems. The 2026 Rasuwa disaster in the Nepal Himalaya highlights the destructive potential of these cascading processes, in which a massive rock–ice avalanche transformed into a devastating downstream flood and sediment-laden flow. This event is referred to as a “Himalayan tsunami” because the rapidly propagating flood and debris-flow wave resembled the destructive waves of an oceanic tsunami. Similar, although comparatively smaller, disasters have occurred across the Himalaya, including the Seti River disaster in Pokhara, Nepal, on 5 May 2012; the Bhotekoshi disaster in Sindhupalchowk, Nepal, in July 2016; the Chamoli disaster in India on 7 February 2021; the Melamchi disaster in Nepal on 15 June 2021; and the Sikkim disaster in India on 3 October 2023. Together, these events demonstrate how high-altitude mass movements and hydrological processes can propagate through mountain river systems, threatening downstream settlements and critical infrastructure. Based on satellite imagery, available field observations, photographs, and geomorphological interpretation, this study examines the source characteristics, cascading processes, and environmental implications of the Rasuwa disaster. Rapid fragmentation and movement, combined with river interaction and the entrainment of sediment and water, provide a reasonable mechanism for the destructive downstream flood and debris-flow wave. The event underscores the limitations of isolated, single-hazard assessments and downstream-focused monitoring. Effective risk reduction requires integrated source-to-sink (S2S) investigations, high-altitude slope materials and glacier monitoring, real-time river observation, transboundary data sharing, impact-based early-warning systems, and risk-sensitive infrastructur

papers.title: Data Fusion for Modelling the Bed Topography of Rock Glacier
papers.summary: The methodology presented in this study was applied to the Bonnard rock glacier, located in southwestern Switzerland between 3000 and 3200 m a.s.l., corresponding to the regional lower limit of permafrost occurrence. The terminal part of the rock glacier constitutes a major source area for recurrent debris flows affecting the downstream Pétérey and Tracuit torrents. To reconstruct the geometry of the stable bedrock surface beneath the rock glacier, several complementary datasets were integrated, including high-resolution LiDAR and photogrammetric topography, seismic refraction surveys, destructive boreholes, geomorphological mapping, and GNSS displacement measurements. All datasets were integrated within a common 3D reference framework using AdHoc-3D software, allowing the generation of a coherent set of georeferenced control points. The resulting dataset was processed using geostatistical interpolation with kriging and external drift to produce a digital elevation model of the bedrock surface. The reconstructed geometry allowed the estimation of the thickness and volume of the active layer, together with associated uncertainties. The results provide quantitative constraints on the potentially mobilizable sediment volumes contributing to debris-flow initiation and therefore constitute a useful tool for hazard assessment and climate-change adaptation in high-alpine periglacial environments.

papers.title: Comparative Model Tests on Deposition Characteristics of Debris Flows under Straight versus Bending Channel Configurations
papers.summary: Debris-flow deposition zones often exhibit evolutionary characteristics such as dispersed sediment particles and a deflected morphology due to changes in flow-path configuration. Current research in this field remains insufficient, constraining hazard prevention and comprehensive utilization of deposition zones. In this study, three types of debris-flow deposits with varying densities were employed as prototype materials. Indoor physical model tests were conducted using a self-developed variable flow-path simulation system under three channel configurations: straight (Type I), single-bend (Type C), and continuous-bend (Type S). By integrating high-speed photography, distributed sensing, and image processing techniques, parameters including flow velocity, discharge, deposition morphology, thickness distribution, and particle size distribution were simultaneously monitored. A deflection angle and offset distance were introduced to quantitatively analyze flow-path deviation behavior. Results show that flow-path morphology dominates deposition patterns: straight channels form strip-like deposits, while curved channels produce fan-shaped distributions. Deposited particles display longitudinal sorting, with finer grains near the flow path and coarser grains farther away; bends significantly hinder the transport of fine particles. Path deviation is primarily controlled by channel morphology, while flow velocity and material density play regulatory roles at specific stages. This study provides a scientific basis for the hazard assessment and engineering design of debris-flow mitigation measures under complex flow paths in mountainous regions.

papers.title: Clast arrangement influences fracture stratigraphy in a carbonate toe-of-slope megabreccia, Permian Rader Member, Bell Canyon Formation, Guadalupe Mountains, Texas, USA
papers.summary: Debris-dominated carbonate slopes comprise extensive volumes of margin-derived lithoclastic and skeletal components. While reefal margins and their steep slopes have been extensively studied and are actively targeted for hydrocarbon production, lower-angle distal slope settings remain less explored. Thus, there are limited insights into depositional processes, stratigraphic architecture, and fracture distribution within these settings, which all strongly influence fluid flow in the subsurface. To address these knowledge gaps, outcrop data were studied from the middle Rader Member megabreccia, a Permian carbonate toe-of-slope deposit exposed in Bell Canyon, Guadalupe Mountains, west Texas, USA. Multiscale sedimentological and structural observations, integrating drone-based digital outcrop models, photomosaics, scanlines, detailed graphic logs, and a novel square-meter grid-cell mapping method, were used to quantify internal architecture, clast-size distribution, matrix composition, and fracture patterns. The studied outcrop, up to 25 m thick and exposed along ~700 m of depositional dip, exhibits repetitive lateral thinning caused by basal erosion and thickening due to the stacking of lithoclasts. Clast-size distributions show inverse grading of megaclasts (boulders exceeding 0.5 m) and normal grading of smaller clasts, along with repetitive downslope coarsening-to-fining patterns influenced by the presence of megaclasts. These observations suggest that the deposit at the studied locality was emplaced as a single event by a granular debris flow (i.e., a grain flow) with abundant particle collisions that promoted inverse grading of megaclasts. Two fracture sets are present in the megabreccia, striking NE-SW and NW-SE, with broadly comparable dimensions and intensity. Fractures are rarely longer or taller than 0.5 m, with high aspect ratios, reflecting strong architectural confinement imposed by the inversely graded structure of the deposit. papers.title: Conditional Root-Stress Exceedance of a 220 kV Disconnect Switch Under Dynamic Slurry–Boulder Debris-Flow Loading
papers.summary: Distributed slurry pressure and local boulder pulses can induce transient stresses in outdoor disconnect switches. This study evaluates conditional root-stress exceedance in an idealized 220 kV disconnect-switch model with prescribed geometry, tied connections, fixed bases, equivalent linear-elastic materials, and separately imposed load histories. Four fixed screening levels of 165, 235, 282, and 375 MPa were considered. The original coarse-mesh (N1) archive contains 213 distinct loading cases, including 100 combined-load cases at four prescribed heights and matched component, height, and load-model checks. The primary demand is the maximum von Mises invariant of the tensor averaged at the original monitored root point. The same 100 combined-load cases were evaluated on the G3H3 and G4H4 meshes in a paired comparison. From G3H3 to G4H4, the median absolute point-demand change was 4.87%, the maximum relative change in the fitted median exceedance velocity was 2.45%, and the largest same-velocity exceedance-probability difference was 21.85 percentage points. The primary curves exceeded the proposed numerical sensitivity targets. The point demands increased by 23.43–27.72% from N1 to G4H4, demonstrating the mesh dependence of the original results. A fixed-volume tensor response was more stable, but remains supplementary and does not validate the point metric. The pressure-redistribution checks used two selected scenarios, and the component comparisons at the two greater heights used eight matched cases per height. These checks illustrate numerical sensitivity and case-specific differences within the N1 reference model; they do not constitute a comprehensive uncertainty analysis or establish physical failure probabilities. This exploratory numerical case study quantifies stress-screening sensitivity within the adopted idealization rather than reconstructing a specific installed unit. papers.title: Trigger–Cause Cross-Attention (TCA)
papers.source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.summary: Trigger–Cause Cross-Attention (TCA) is a deep learning framework for regional debris-flow early warning. It separately represents antecedent hydrometeorological conditions and catchment susceptibility (Cause) and short-term rainfall forcing (Trigger). Cross-attention uses the integrated Cause representation as the Query and the Trigger sequence as the Key and Value, allowing the model to evaluate rainfall forcing conditional on the catchment state. This software release provides a PyTorch implementation of TCA, including masked-reconstruction pretraining, supervised multi-task training, prediction, and a minimal input–output example with real samples. Debris-flow occurrence is the primary prediction task, supported by auxiliary magnitude regression. Exported representations and attention weights support analysis of state-dependent triggering and the temporal relevance of rainfall.

papers.title: UAV LiDAR-based identification method for valley-type debris flows in southeastern Tibet
papers.source: International Conference on Advances in Energy and Environmental Engineering (AEEE)
papers.summary: The southeastern Tibetan Plateau is characterized by deeply incised alpine valleys, steep terrain, and dense vegetation with strong spatial heterogeneity. These landscape conditions can hinder the identification of valley-type debris-flow deposits from optical imagery, especially when older fans are partly obscured by forest or when their spectral differences from the surrounding ground surface have weakened over time. To address this limitation, the Duoxiongla Valley was selected as the study area, and high-resolution topographic information was acquired using UAV-based LiDAR. Hillshade maps generated from the LiDAR-derived terrain data were used to assist the detailed interpretation of debris-flow fan morphology. The analysis primarily targeted fan deposits concealed by vegetation. Interpretation was based on fan- or tongue-shaped landforms near gully outlets, together with subtle topographic variations that remained detectable beneath the forest canopy. Optical imagery was used as supplementary evidence to check upstream channel connectivity, erosional traces, and exposed coarse materials such as gravels and boulders. The results indicate that UAV LiDAR can reveal the microtopographic form of debris-flow fans that are difficult to distinguish in optical imagery, especially in forested valley sections. A total of 48 historical debris-flow fans were identified in the study area, including 32 on the southern slope and 16 on the northern slope of the Duoxiongla River. This pattern suggests a clear aspect-related asymmetry in the distribution of debris-flow fans. The results provide useful basic data for valley-type debris-flow investigation and hazard inventory construction in southeastern Tibet.

papers.title: A novel soil-water characteristic curve prediction model for unsaturated soil considering pore structure characteristics
papers.summary: The soil-water characteristic curve (SWCC) graphically describes the significant hydraulic characteristics of unsaturated soil seepage. Several factors influence the SWCC of unsaturated soil, including temperature, void ratio, pore characteristics, particle composition, and load, with soil pore structure exerting a pivotal influence on SWCC. This study aimed to analyze the influence of pore structure on the SWCC of loess. The results showed that the shape of SWCC of loess is similar with varying pore structures under a fixed void ratio, with discrepancies in the air entry value(AEV) and decline sections. The void ratio of macro pores of intact loess exceeded that of remolded loess, in turn resulting in a larger AEV. There were fewer small pores and middle pores in the intact loess sample, whereas the remolded loess showed a greater decline rate after transitioning into an the unsaturated state. On the other hand, an increase in the size of the pores was observed in the loess following the drying-wetting cycles, whereas the number of smaller and middle-sized pores decreased. Similarly, there was an increase in AEV of loess following the drying-wetting cycles, with the gradual deceleration in the rate of decline in the unsaturated stage. The pore state parameters and fractal dimension of pore size distribution(PSD) were introduced into the V-G model based on the experimental results, with deriving a modified V-G model. The intact loess was predicted by remolded loess, and the loess after the drying-wetting cycles were predicted by loess before the drying-wetting cycles. The results showed that the modified V-G model is more effective in predicting the SWCC of intact loess and loess after the drying-wetting cycles.

papers.title: Modeling Seasonal Shrink-Swell and Saturated Zone Deformation of Clay Underneath Buildings on Shallow Foundations
papers.summary: Increased damage reporting for residential buildings in the Netherlands following recent droughts has incentivized applied laboratory, field, and modeling investigations of the role of seasonal deformation of clay underneath buildings on shallow foundations. Here, a mathematical model is presented which simulates water transport, water content changes and deformation in the saturated and unsaturated zone at the building scale. The model provides a process-based framework to improve understanding of hydro-mechanical soil-foundation interaction in clay-rich settings, and to clarify factors that contribute to damage risk. Water loss and gain from evapotranspiration and rainfall drive the model and are applied adjacent to the building. Effects extend underneath the building and the (phreatic) water table movements are simulated rather than imposed. Shrink-swell and saturated zone deformation are modeled as a reversible process. A unique feature of the formulation lies in the extension of the van Genuchten retention model toward stress-dependent behavior, establishing formal continuity between unsaturated retention physics and the saturated compressibility framework conventionally employed in geotechnical practice. This allows exploring effects of the weight of the building. Laboratory-determined retention, hydraulic conductivity and shrinkage curves are used to model the differential vertical movements.

papers.title: Analytical Analysis of VOC Remediation by Horizontal Permeable Reactive Barriers for Time-Dependent Source
papers.source: Boletim da Sociedade Paranaense de Matemática
papers.summary: Various natural and man-made objects, like industrial waste buried beneath soil emit many harmful gases known as Volatile Organic Compounds (VOCs) are hazardous for living beings. If released in environment VOCs can contaminate air, soil, and groundwater, causing health risks like dizziness, organ damage, and cancer. Their migration through unsaturated soil occurs via diffusion, advection and dispersion. Horizontal Permeable Reactive Barriers (HPRBs) are an effective in situ method to remediate and oxidize VOCs in the vadose zone. The degradation of an HPRB due to long-term interaction with VOCs occurs over several years; therefore, mathematical modeling is an effective and necessary tool for predicting its long-term behavior, as conducting experiments over such extended timescales in real life is impractical. In this study, an analytical diffusion-reaction model is presented to investigate VOC transport from a subsurface source, through the unsaturated soil layer, and into a HPRB. The model accounts for time-dependent conditions and the transport process is analyzed separately under the effects of various parameters involved. The obtained simulation through graph shows good agreement with the behavior observed in experiment. This study provides insight into the long-term performance and durability of the HPRB, which will help in barrier design and lifetime assessment.

papers.title: SHEAR RESPONSE OF UNSATURATED CLAY–GEOTEXTILE INTERFACE UNDER A WIDE RANGE OF SUCTIONS
papers.source: Digital Repository at the University of Maryland (University of Maryland College Park)
papers.summary: Soil–geotextile interface behavior governs the performance of many geotechnical systems, including mechanically stabilized earth walls, reinforced slopes, pavements, embankments, and landfill cover systems. Although the behavior of these interfaces has been widely investigated under saturated conditions, their response under unsaturated conditions remains insufficiently understood, particularly at medium- to high-suction levels encountered in compacted fine-grained soils. Most previous studies have been limited to low matric suctions (<100–300 kPa), leaving a gap in understanding interface behavior under higher suction conditions representative of many field environments.This research investigates the shear behavior of unsaturated low-plasticity clay–geotextile interfaces over a suction range of 1 to 8 MPa using two low-plasticity clay soils and two polypropylene geotextiles (woven and nonwoven). The experimental program included soil-water retention curve (SWRC) testing using the osmotic method, suction measurements using the filter paper method, and direct shear testing conducted under normal stresses of 50, 100, and 200 kPa. The study evaluates the influence of suction, normal stress, soil type, and geotextile type on the peak and post-peak interface shear behavior. The experimental results show that interface shear strength increases with increasing suction; however, the relationship is nonlinear and cannot be adequately represented by conventional linear extensions of the Mohr–Coulomb failure criterion. The increase in shear strength is primarily attributed to suction-induced adhesion, while the interface friction angle remains nearly constant throughout the investigated suction range. Nonwoven geotextiles consistently mobilized greater suction-dependent interface resistance than woven geotextiles because of their greater contact area and enhanced soil–fiber interaction. The results also demonstrate that suction influences both peak and residual interface behav

papers.title: A hyper-reduction strategy for elastoplastic hydro-mechanical problems in partially saturated soil
papers.summary: This work proposes a hyper-reduced order model for coupled hydro-mechanical simulations of elastoplastic deformation and water flow in partially saturated soils. These simulations are used to monitor and assess the safety of geotechnical structures such as earthfill dams, where calibration, uncertainty quantification and scenario analysis require solving the same transient model many times for different parameter values. The displacement and the pore pressure are approximated in a field-split reduced basis obtained by proper orthogonal decomposition, and the Galerkin-projected equations are integrated with decomposed cubature rules, one per balance equation, built with the energy-conserving sampling and weighting (ECSW) method. Each residual is split into an affine part and a nonlinear correction: the affine part is computed exactly, at negligible online cost, so that the cubature rule only needs to approximate the correction, which is localized in space. The construction is independent of the constitutive model choices and is implemented in FEniCSx by assembling the original variational forms on the small set of elements selected by ECSW. The method is tested on two- and three-dimensional dams retaining tailings and water, simulating a raise of the dam and the subsequent consolidation phase, with the friction angle, stiffness and hydraulic conductivity of the dam material and the height of the raise as varying parameters. The hyper-reduced model reproduces the displacement and pressure fields with errors below $0.5\%$ with respect to the finite element solution, achieving speed-ups of up to $43\times$ in two dimensions and $77\times$ in three. These performance gains grow with the extent of the plastic yielding, and the selected elements concentrate in the plastified and unsaturated zones, whose size is set by the physics rather than by the mesh resolution.

papers.summary: Python Scripting for PLAXIS is a comprehensive guide to developing Python-based workflows for automating PLAXIS analyses, enabling increased productivity, reduced errors and more efficient use of engineering effort in geotechnical modeling. PLAXIS is a widely used finite element software for analyzing safety, stability, deformation, consolidation and groundwater flow problems in geotechnical engineering. It is routinely applied to complex projects such as foundations, dams, embankments, ground improvement, and both surface and underground excavations. While most users rely on the graphical user interface (GUI), PLAXIS also provides powerful scripting capabilities through its command-line interface and Python API. This book demonstrates how these capabilities can be leveraged to automate repetitive modeling and analysis tasks, streamline workflows and enhance consistency in model definition and execution. Written for researchers, academics and practicing engineers alike, the book is ideal for both new and experienced PLAXIS users seeking to integrate scripting into their daily workflows and unlock the full potential of the software.

papers.title: Effects of sequential hydration on water retention and shrinkage of cement-stabilized unsaturated soil
papers.summary: Early-age shrinkage cracking often compromises the durability of infrastructures constructed with cement–stabilized soils (CSS). This study evaluates a sequential hydration (SH) strategy designed to curb shrinkage while sustaining hydraulic response (e.g., degree of saturation) and mechanical performance pertinent to seepage control and serviceability limit-state design. Three hydration paths were examined: OH-100, one-time hydration at 100 % OMC; SH-80 and SH-60, compaction at 80 % and 60 % OMC respectively, followed by second-stage wetting. Soil-water retention curves (SWRCs) were measured under zero-stress and vertical stress using a stress-controllable pressure-plate apparatus and drying–wetting shrinkage was tracked over three cycles for a CSS. The results show that SH significantly reduces early-age free shrinkage while modifying water-retention behavior, hysteresis, and stress-dependent hydraulic response. Among the investigated treatments, SH at 80 % OMC produced the most favorable balance between shrinkage mitigation and hydraulic performance. SEM/EDX analyses suggest that staged hydration promotes pore-throat refinement and changes hydration-product distribution, particularly A-S-H formation. These findings indicate that SH may serve as a construction-stage strategy for reducing shrinkage cracking in cement-treated pavement bases while maintaining adequate hydraulic performance.

papers.title: Evidence for temporal decoupling of olivine weathering and inorganic carbon removal in unsaturated soil columns
papers.summary: Introduction Enhanced Rock Weathering (ERW) is a nature-based carbon dioxide (CO 2 ) removal technology that speeds the natural weathering process of rocks by applying finely ground silicate rocks over the land surface. It has been proposed that ERW can remove between 0.5 and 2 Gt CO 2 year −1 when deployed at scale. To investigate how soil porewater responds to the dissolution of silicate dust during enhanced rock weathering, we conducted unsaturated soil column experiments amended with olivine (Mg 2 SiO 4 ). Methods Since the main principle of ERW-based carbon removal is the reaction of atmospheric CO 2 dissolved in rainwater with silicate rocks, leading to release of base cations and bicarbonate ions, we measured cations, anions, pH, alkalinity, dissolved inorganic carbon (DIC) and dissolved organic carbon (DOC) in the leached effluent. Complementary solid-phase soil measurements of exchangeable cations, pH, total inorganic carbon (TIC) and total organic carbon (TOC) were performed to improve understanding of weathering product transport and retention, while aqueous speciation calculations provided saturation state information of relevant secondary mineral phases. Results We demonstrate that measurable olivine weathering can occur without proportional short-term export of bicarbonate or DIC, and estimates of potential CO 2 removal based on weathering-derived cation release exceeded realized inorganic CO 2 removal quantified from bicarbonate and DIC export. Furthermore, the observed increase in DOC export and decrease in surface-soil organic carbon suggest that enhanced weathering may alter soil organic carbon dynamics. papers.title: Temperature-dependent swelling and compressibility behavior of microfiber-reinforced bentonite
papers.summary: Abstract Bentonite is widely used as a buffer material in deep geological repositories because its low hydraulic conductivity and swelling pressure help limit advective radionuclide transport. Elevated temperature, however, can cause drying and shrinkage, which may alter swelling behavior and reduce mechanical integrity. Fiber reinforcement has been proposed to mitigate these effects, but the behavior of fiber-reinforced bentonite at elevated temperature remains poorly understood. This study investigates the swelling pressure, compressibility, and consolidation behavior of glass microfiber-reinforced Na-bentonite at 22 °C and 50 °C with fiber contents of 0, 1, and 3 wt%. The fiber sensitivity of swelling pressure decreased by 42% over the 28 K temperature increase, from − 72.9 kPa/wt% at 22 °C to − 42.5 kPa/wt% at 50 °C, even though the overall swelling pressure increased with temperature. To interpret the results, a thermo-Barcelona Basic Model (BBM) framework with a volumetric homogenization fiber composite term was calibrated against the experimental data. The analysis indicates that the reduced fiber sensitivity at elevated temperature is mainly related to a decrease in the apparent fiber–matrix interfacial bond strength, τ b , from 16 to 9 kPa, whereas the bentonite-phase parameters λ(0) and p 0 changed only slightly. These findings suggest that the effectiveness of fiber reinforcement depends not only on fiber properties, but also on the thermal stability of the fiber–clay interface under hydrothermal conditions. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) observations showed fiber–clay contact and clay coating on fiber surfaces, supporting the proposed interfacial mechanism. Overall, the results suggest that interfacial bond stability should be considered when selecting inorganic fiber reinforcement for engineered barrier materials subjected to coupled thermo-hydro-mechanical conditions.

papers.title: Toward Hydrogeophysical Digital Twins for Sustainable Rice Intensification: A Systematic Review of Electrical Resistivity Tomography, Physics-Informed Machine Learning, and Decision-Support Architectures
papers.summary: Sustainable rice production requires improved understanding and management of soil–water dynamics, particularly under water-saving irrigation practices. Conventional monitoring approaches often provide limited information about the spatial and temporal variability of subsurface hydrological conditions. Emerging developments in electrical resistivity tomography (ERT), physics-informed machine learning (PIML), and digital twin technologies offer promising opportunities to improve subsurface monitoring, hydrological modeling, and adaptive irrigation decision-making. This systematic literature review aims to critically examine the scientific evidence supporting the development of hydrogeophysical digital twins for sustainable rice intensification. Rather than assuming that ERT, physics-informed modeling, and digital twin technologies have already been fully integrated into rice production systems, the review will evaluate their individual capabilities, existing technological linkages, integration maturity, methodological limitations, and potential transferability. The review will focus on four interrelated research domains: (1) hydrogeophysical monitoring using ERT, including time-lapse ERT and related resistivity-based approaches; (2) physics-informed machine learning and hybrid physics–data modeling of soil moisture, unsaturated flow, and root water uptake; (3) digital twin architectures, data integration, and decision-support systems for agricultural water management; and (4) hydrological, agronomic, environmental, socioeconomic, and operational requirements of sustainable rice intensification, including the System of Rice Intensification (SRI) and alternate wetting and drying (AWD). Studies directly investigating rice-based production systems will be prioritized. papers.title: Generalized Effective Stress Equation for Variably Saturated Frozen Soil
papers.source: Journal of Geotechnical and Geoenvironmental Engineering
papers.summary: Abstract A unified effective stress equation for variably saturated frozen soil is proposed, theoretically verified, and experimentally evaluated. Cryostress, capillary suction stress, and adsorptive suction stress coexist when variably saturated soil is subject to freezing and thawing. Cryostress consists of three physically distinct forces at three interfaces: ice–ice bonding, ice–liquid capillary force, and ice–particle adsorptive force. Cryostress is a characteristic function of temperature and water content quantified by the cryostress characteristic curve. A generalized effective stress can be established by applying the principles of mechanical equilibrium and soil water potential equilibrium on the soil–water–ice–air representative element volume. A closed-form equation is developed where effective stress is equal to the total stress minus suction stress and cryostress. The generalized effective stress equation can be reduced to Bishop’s form of effective stress in saturated frozen soil when ice–particle adsorptive stress is neglected, to Lu and Likos’ suction stress-based effective stress in unfrozen unsaturated soil, and to Terzaghi’s effective stress in unfrozen saturated soil. The closed-form equation is experimentally evaluated using published shear strength test results for sandy soil, lean clay, and silty clay. The fitted parameters also show good consistency with independently measured soil water and soil freezing characteristic curves for lean clay. The proposed framework offers a practical and unified approach to describe the strength of variably saturated frozen soils.

Soil cores (Herndon silt loam with a barley straw) were packed at two bulk densities (1.16 g cm −3 and 0.78 g cm −3 ) to create contrasting pore size distributions. Following saturation, water was selectively removed from specific pore size classes using the pressure plate desorption method at 4, 10, or 100 kPa. Additional treatments for pore water manipulation included unsaturated soil control without water manipulation and wet soil control, i.e., soil subjected to free drainage under open air after saturation. These pore size and moisture manipulations created different pore size classes with varying moistures. Both microbial diversity and community composition were associated with pore size distributions (i.e., bulk density), pore water manipulation, and sampling time. By taking advantage of both soil moisture change and microbial succession during barley straw decomposition, we used the ratio of microbial taxa or predicted functions between day 38 and day 10 of the incubation to infer microbial preferences for specific pore size classes. If microbial distribution had no pore size preference, the ratios for abundance change on day 38 to day 10 should be similar among soils subjected to different pore size and moisture manipulations. papers.title: The 7 April 2026 Reactivation of the Petacciato Landslide (Adriatic Coast, Italy): Field Evidence, Ground Deformation, and Rainfall-Triggering Conditions
papers.summary: The Petacciato landslide is a well-known, very large landslide located along the Adriatic coast of central–southern Italy and involving Plio-Pleistocene marine clay sequences with sandy intercalations. Reactivations have been documented since the early twentieth century and have occurred predominantly after prolonged rainfall periods. On 7 April 2026, a new reactivation event provided an opportunity to investigate this complex landslide system further. Displacements affected the A14 motorway and the Adriatic railway and led to the declaration of a national state of emergency. This study integrates geological, geomorphological, and hydrological information with recent European Ground Motion Service (EGMS) remote-sensing data and precipitation analyses to improve the understanding of the phenomenon. The findings indicate that the Apennine thrust front acts as a structural predisposing factor for the deep-seated landslide, whereas prolonged rainfall triggers reactivation. The analysis highlights the role of long-term cumulative rainfall as a primary driver of reactivation and the value of InSAR monitoring for evaluating continuous ground deformation, including during apparently dormant periods. The results emphasise how reactivation events can improve understanding of landslide behaviour and inform risk-management strategies.

papers.title: From Rainfall to Absolute Landslide Probability: A Machine Learning–Based Approach
papers.summary: Abstract Landslides are prevalent geological hazards in mountainous and hilly regions, posing significant threats to human lives, property, and infrastructure, especially when external factors such as heavy rainfall elevate the risk of occurrence. In recent years, the rapid development of remote sensing technology, geographic information system, and big data analytics has enabled the establishment of landslide databases and the refinement of landslide hazard assessment methodologies, opening new avenues for disaster prediction and prevention research. This study focuses on the probabilistic hazard assessment of rainfall-induced landslides, using the heavy rainfall event in Nanping City, Fujian, in 2019 as a case study. The absolute probability of landslide occurrence was quantified by integrating machine learning models with Bayesian probability theory. To analyze their contributions to landslide hazard, the study comprehensively considered nine key factors: elevation, slope angle, slope aspect, topographic wetness index, fault distance, rainfall amount, topographic position index, land cover, and stratum. The findings reveal that rainfall intensity is the primary trigger for landslides. However, the occurrence of landslides also depends on the combined influence of topography, geology, and human activities rather than rainfall alone. Building on these insights, this study extends the established landslide probability assessment model to a wider region. And simulating landslide occurrence probabilities under various rainfall scenarios. This approach confirms the strong correlation between rainfall and landslides while offering scientific support for emergency management and disaster warning systems. The research provides a robust foundation for disaster prevention and control in mountainous areas, infrastructure planning, and the development of emergency response systems, particularly by refining landslide prediction models that account for multiple factors. papers.title: A real-time visual monitoring method for landslide creep using platform attitude self-calibration
papers.summary: High-frequency, high-precision, real-time displacement monitoring is essential for early warning of landslide creep, a key precursor to slope failure. However, platform attitude disturbances, such as wind-induced vibration and foundation settlement, can introduce spurious displacement into image sequences and reduce the accuracy of conventional vision-based monitoring. This study proposes a real-time visual monitoring technique for landslide creep based on platform attitude self-calibration. An optical tracker and an inertial measurement unit were integrated to acquire target images and attitude data simultaneously. A displacement decomposition model incorporating attitude fluctuations was developed to separate true slope movement from attitude-induced spurious displacement. Subpixel target localization used gradient-direction voting and weighted elliptical fitting, and real-time attitude estimation used an error-state Kalman filter. Indoor vibration tests at 40 m achieved an RMSE below 0.7 mm, with reductions of 0.955 and 0.846 compared with vision-only and vision-plus-reference-point correction approaches, respectively. During a 93-day field campaign at the Dayangshan landslide, Suzhou, the approach achieved a data capture rate of 0.986, an RMSE of 0.28–0.36 mm, and a correlation coefficient above 0.91 versus GNSS data. The approach provides a practical option for early warning of slope failure by accurately and continuously monitoring landslide creep under unstable platform conditions and unfavorable weather.

papers.title: A GeoAI framework for landslide susceptibility mapping using Google Earth Engine, ensemble machine learning, and SHAP explainable AI
papers.summary: Landslides are among the most destructive natural hazards in mountainous regions, yet susceptibility mapping in data-scarce areas remains challenging. This study proposes a reproducible Geospatial Artificial Intelligence (GeoAI) framework that integrates Google Earth Engine (GEE), ensemble machine learning, and explainable AI (XAI) for landslide susceptibility mapping in central Nepal. Using a balanced dataset of 9,479 observations from 4,743 landslide and 4,736 non-landslide locations, extracted seven conditioning factors: topographic (elevation, slope, aspect), climatic (rainfall), ecological (NDVI, land cover), and anthropogenic (population density) within the GEE cloud computing environment. Random Forest (RF) and Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) models using stratified train-test splitting and 10-fold cross-validation. Both models showed strong predictive performance, with XGBoost achieving superior results (Accuracy: 88.3%, ROC-AUC: 0.952) compared to RF (Accuracy: 87.9%, ROC-AUC: 0.945). SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) identified slope as the most influential predictor associated with model predictions followed by rainfall (16%) and elevation (15%), while lower NDVI values consistently correlated with higher susceptibility. The susceptibility map identified high-risk zones concentrated in Sindhupalchok, Dolakha, Dhading, Rasuwa, Gorkha, and Nuwakot districts. This framework reveals that freely available satellite data, cloud computing, and explainable machine learning can be effectively integrated for susceptibility mapping and community resilience initiatives.

papers.title: Stability Assessment of Landslides under Coupling Action of Rainfall and Earthquake
papers.summary: Abstract Separated analyses are widely used to evaluate the stability of slopes after rainfall and earthquakes. However, the combined impact of rainfall infiltration and earthquake shaking on slope stability remains insufficiently studied. Therefore, a unique closed-form analytical solution to calculate the factor of safety (FS) for homogeneous unsaturated slopes under combined seepage and seismic forces has been proposed by modifying the conventional Bishop’s method. The two-dimensional seepage pattern was considered to capture rainfall infiltration, while pseudo-dynamic forces at each failure slice accounted for earthquake shaking. Further, an analytical search method was developed to locate the critical slip surface. Additionally, a coupled hydromechanical finite-element model was used to analyze rainfall-induced seepage, deformation, and stress redistribution. The resulting slope condition was further evaluated under seismic loading to represent rainfall–earthquake effects without implying full two-way coupling between infiltration and earthquake shaking. All these newly proposed methodologies were applied to the 2014 Malin landslide in Maharashtra, India, to replicate the landslide mechanism and identify root causes to show the application of proposed analytical solutions. A comparison with field observations and literature demonstrated that both the analytical and numerical models realistically represented the Malin landslide. Further, the proposed analytical model was validated against a numerical analysis of a real earthquake-induced landslide. The models accurately reproduced the onset, failure zone, and progression of instability over time. The present study provides the application of new analytical solutions for practical landslides, additionally offering a reference for prevention and evacuation plans.

papers.title: LeMoRe-MTKD: A Multi-Teacher–Student Knowledge Distillation Deep Learning Framework for Landslide Segmentation Using UAV Imagery
papers.summary: Landslides (LSs) are a natural phenomenon, typically triggered by heavy rainfall and earthquakes, and pose a global danger to human lives and property. LSs frequently occur on steep slopes and in loose soil conditions, and damaged sites can be hard to reach thereafter. Thus, remote approaches would be relevant and practical for investigations, and the use of an Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) for imaging, along with robust methods to identify and quantify LS-affected areas, is recommended. Therefore, this study proposed a multi-teacher–student knowledge distillation (KD) deep learning framework for landslide semantic segmentation. The lightweight LeMoRe model is selected for the learner model (student), and SegNet, U-Net, DeepLabV3+, and LinkNet are used as the teacher networks. To establish the UAV training dataset, we conducted UAV imaging for four LS sites, including Mogo, Buri, Oejeong, and Sangneung (testing site) villages, in Sancheong County, South Korea, in 2025. First, all plain networks are trained on the training dataset, and then KD is applied for single-teacher and multi-teacher KD. Subsequently, ablation studies are implemented to identify the optimal KD component set and the best student–teacher combination (with equal weights) for subsequent experiments. In addition, the equal-weight combination is tuned for the optimal teacher weight proportion to maximize the teacher knowledge transfer to the student. The best model weight is saved for inference with the testing site of Sangneung to map the LS-damaged areas. The experiment results reveal an improvement in accuracy (6.3% F1, 8.2% IoU with equal weight and 12.3% F1 and around 16.8% IoU with the tuned weight). The inference results for the Sangneung testing site were qualitatively and quantitatively evaluated through visual comparison with the original UAV imagery with three zoom-in areas presented for detailed examination. papers.title: Multiobjective Optimization of Landslide Rheological Parameters Based on Random Forest and Nondominated Sorting Genetic Algorithm II
papers.summary: Abstract Rheological parameters (e.g., pore pressure coefficient r u and dynamic friction angle ϕ ) are necessary input for landslide runout evaluation. However, due to high randomness of initiation, propagation, and accumulation, it is impossible to directly measure rheological properties. This study proposes an optimization method for calibrating landslide rheological parameters based on random forest (RF) and Nondominated Sorting Genetic Algorithm II (NSGA-II). Firstly, a dynamic numerical model of landslide is established using three-dimensional model DAN (DAN3D). Then, the lateral accumulation width and the longitudinal runout distance at different spatial locations across the deposit are integrated to calibrate the rheological parameters. Next, the NSGA-II algorithm is employed to obtain the Pareto solutions of rheological parameters by minimizing the prediction errors of lateral and longitudinal runout characteristics at each location. To avoid extensive repetitive DAN3D simulations within NSGA-II, RF-based surrogate models are established to estimate the lateral and longitudinal runout characteristics at different spatial locations. The final optimal rheological parameters are objectively selected from Pareto solutions by the entropy weight method (EWM). Finally, the proposed approaches are illustrated and validated using two landslides that occurred in Gansu Province, China. Results indicated that rheological parameters optimized by the proposed approaches not only can accurately characterize the endangered area of historical events, but also provide reasonable forward prediction of runout behavior of similar landslide events with desired accuracy. RF surrogate models can remove the computational burden within NSGA-II. Integrating both the lateral accumulation width and longitudinal runout distance into the calibration of rheological parameters can improve the prediction accuracy of landslide endangered area.

papers.title: Recurrent Landslide Hazards in Ramban District, NW Himalaya, India: An Interplay of Geology, Climate Change, and Anthropogenic Factors
papers.summary: Abstract Landslide hazards along the Banihal–Ramban corridor of the Jammu–Srinagar National Highway (NH-44) represent a critical geoenvironmental challenge in Northwestern Himalaya, where active tectonics, fragile lithology, steep terrain, and increasing extreme precipitation interact with intensive infrastructure development. This technical note presents a focused analysis of flash floods and landslides of April 20, 2025, examining their triggering mechanisms, cascading geomorphic processes, and impacts on transportation infrastructure and settlements. Historical landslide records (1990–2025) and regional hydroclimatic observations are incorporated to contextualize the event within evolving patterns of hazard frequency and anthropogenic slope modification along the NH-44 corridor. The April 2025 disaster resulted from the localized high-intensity precipitation, which elevated pore-water pressures, reduced slope stability, and triggered multiple failures in structurally weakened rock formations. Results highlight a transition from isolated slope failures toward compound and cascading hazard scenarios involving flash floods, debris flows, and infrastructure disruption. The study underscores the increasing vulnerability of this strategic Himalayan lifeline. It emphasizes the need for geologically informed engineering design, improved drainage management, and integrated early warning strategies to enhance long-term resilience.

papers.title: Numerical Simulation of Landslide-Generated Waves in Reservoirs Using a Coupled SPH-DCDEM Method
papers.summary: Abstract Landslide-generated waves occur when sliding masses impact the water surface, potentially posing significant hazards to nearby areas. This study utilizes the smoothed particle hydrodynamics–distributed contact discrete-element method (SPH-DCDEM) coupling module within DualSPHysics to simulate landslide-generated waves in reservoirs, where the SPH method models the fluid flow and the DCDEM method captures the dynamics of the granular landslide mass. The accuracy and effectiveness of the SPH-DCDEM method in simulating landslide-generated waves are validated using two physical model experiments of subaerial landslide-generated waves. Using a simplified representation of a reservoir bank deposit at the RuMei (RM) Hydropower Station in China, this study conducts an in-depth analysis elucidating the key parameters that control landslide-generated waves in reservoirs. It is found that landslide thickness and landslide entry velocity are the primary controlling factors for two-dimensional granular landslides. Empirical formulas for predicting the maximum wave height and maximum run-up height for the RongSong (RS) landslide deposit at the RM Hydropower Station are developed. The results highlight the potential for more concentrated energy and greater destructive power in landslide-generated waves in mountainous reservoirs compared to those in open water areas.

papers.title: Integrating Kernel-Based Machine Learning Techniques with Geospatial Analysis for Landslide Susceptibility Mapping in Sikkim, India
papers.source: Journal of Computing in Civil Engineering
papers.summary: Abstract Landslides are among the most destructive natural hazards, causing substantial loss of life and infrastructure, particularly in mountainous regions. Accurate identification of landslide-prone areas remains challenging due to complex and nonlinear interactions among geological, topographical, and environmental factors. This study evaluates kernel-based machine learning approaches, namely, kernel logistic regression (KLR) and support vector machine (SVM), for landslide susceptibility mapping (LSM) in Sikkim, India. A balanced data set comprising 693 landslide and 695 nonlandslide samples was constructed using 15 conditioning factors representing topographic, hydrological, environmental, geological, and seismic conditions. The grid search method was utilized to identify optimal hyperparameter configurations. Model performance was quantitatively assessed using accuracy, kappa coefficient, specificity, area under curve (AUC), landslide density, and success rate curve (SRC). The results demonstrate that the KLR with a polynomial kernel (KLR_poly) achieved the highest predictive performance, with an accuracy of 0.741 and an area under curve (AUC) of 0.829, outperforming other KLR variants, while the SVM with an rbf kernel (SVM_rbf) achieved the highest predictive performance, with an accuracy of 0.749 and an AUC of 0.764, outperforming other SVM variants. Furthermore, the landslide density analysis showed a systematic increase in landslide concentration from low to high susceptibility classes for nonlinear models, while SRC results indicated moderate to good predictive capability across all models, confirming effective spatial prioritization of landslide-prone areas. Additionally, a feature importance analysis was conducted to identify the most significant factors influencing landslide occurrence.

papers.title: Landslide identification and susceptibility assessment in high-consequence areas of the oilfield based on multi-band InSAR and machine learning
papers.summary: Loess landslides pose a serious threat to energy infrastructure on the Loess Plateau; however, studies on landslide identification and monitoring in high-consequence areas of oil and gas facilities remain limited. This study investigates landslide identification and susceptibility assessment in a high-consequence area of the Changqing Oilfield in Qingyang City, Gansu Province, China, using Lutan-1 and Sentinel-1 Synthetic Aperture Radar data and machine learning. Combining optical remote sensing images and applying the Minimum Covariance Determinant method and Density-Based Spatial Clustering of Applications with Noise (DBSCAN) to the InSAR derived deformation results, 65 potential landslides are identified. A random forest model, incorporating 13 conditioning factors, is constructed to generate a susceptibility map, with Shapley Additive explanations (SHAP) analysis used to interpret factor contributions. The results indicate that high susceptibility zones are predominantly controlled by surface roughness, distance to streams, and land surface temperature, and contain the majority of identified landslide points. 21.7% of oilfield facilities fall within these high-risk zones, highlighting the urgent need for continuous monitoring. This integrated framework provides a practical approach for geological hazard prevention in loess areas with critical energy infrastructure.

papers.title: Analytical Solutions for Water Infiltration in an Infinite Vegetated Slope under Heavy Rainfall and Its Shallow Stability
papers.summary: Abstract Heavy rainfall is a common natural phenomenon. Regarding the issue of water infiltration in an infinite vegetated slope (consisting of rooted and unrooted layers) under the heavy rainfall condition, the infiltration process is divided into two stages— before and after the slope surface reaches saturation—and the corresponding analytical solutions are acquired through several mathematical approaches. Then the proposed solutions are effectively verified by two comparisons. Finally, based on the factor of safety ( F s ), the effects of key factors on the slope’s shallow stability are quantitatively investigated, and some novel findings are obtained. For example, an increased heavy rainfall rate reduces the F s , but this effect exhibits a tendency of increasing and then decreasing. An increase in transpiration rate enhances the infinite vegetated slope’s whole stability, while its influence will be declined after the heavy rainfall infiltration. The increased root tensile strength improves the F s within the rooted layer, but does not affect the unrooted layer’s stability. Moreover, compared with the “exponential” root shape, the F s within the unrooted layer is slightly lower in the case of the “uniform” root shape. Overall, the findings provide useful insights into infiltration mechanisms and shallow stability of infinite vegetated slopes under heavy rainfalls.

papers.title: Improved Landslide Detection in Southeastern Xizang Based on L-DCGAN-Augmented Data and the L-YOLOv8 Model
papers.summary: Abstract Landslides are common geological disasters that cause extensive damage and significant harm. Efficient recognition of landslide remote sensing images holds both theoretical and practical importance. However, practical landslide detection faces challenges including limited data, high computation, large memory use, and low accuracy. In this study, high-quality landslide remote sensing images were collected from southeastern Xizang to construct a landslide remote sensing data set. To address the issue of insufficient samples, an improved model, landslide-deep convolutional generative adversarial network (L-DCGAN), based on DCGAN, was proposed to enhance landslide remote sensing data. The enhanced data set was constructed by incorporating efficient channel attention (ECA) and squeeze-and-excitation (SE) modules into the generator and discriminator, respectively. Additionally, an improved YOLOv8 model, landslide-you only look once version 8(L-YOLOv8), was proposed. First, the cross-stage partial pyramid convolution (CSPPC) and grouped and shuffled convolution (GSConv) modules replaced the cross stage partial layer with 2 branches (C2f) module and ordinary convolution in the network to reduce the number of model parameters and computational complexity. Then, the spatial and channel synergistic attention (SCSA) mechanism was introduced to improve detection accuracy. Experimental results showed that compared with the original YOLOv8 algorithm, the number of model parameters in L-YOLOv8 was reduced by approximately 41.78%, and the average accuracy on the landslide sample data set was increased by 0.57%, and frames per second (FPS) was improved by 33.87%. The model achieved lightweight design while improving detection speed and accuracy, and demonstrated superior performance on the landslide remote sensing data set.

papers.title: Response and Failure of Los Grillos Bridge to a Slow-Moving Landslide
papers.source: Journal of Structural Design and Construction Practice
papers.summary: Abstract A reconnaissance mission was organized by the American Concrete Institute, Committee 133, to visit the Los Grillos Bridge in Colombia on September 13, 2023. The bridge is a post-tensioned cast-in-place segmental cantilever structure featuring a box girder spanning 180 m. Situated on a slow-moving landslide, the bridge failed on August 20, 2023. Analyses indicated that the concrete crushing of the bottom slab of the 180-m-long box girder triggered the failure. This case study demonstrates that similar structures can withstand large relative deformations in the transverse direction and differential settlements, yet they remain quite vulnerable to displacement in the longitudinal direction. It also highlights the susceptibility of bridge structures in unstable geological regions.

papers.title: Impact of Rainfall Infiltration on Groundwater Seepage under the Effect of Urban Construction in Shanghai
papers.summary: Abstract Groundwater seepage is influenced by various anthropogenic factors during urban construction, among which subsurface structures and surface hardening are two key factors. This study employed numerical simulations to investigate the impacts of rainfall infiltration on groundwater seepage under the effect of urban construction. A numerical model was established to predict groundwater level (GWL) in the phreatic aquifer (Aq0), incorporating the actual distribution of impervious surfaces and subsurface structures for a representative urban area in Shanghai. The model accounted for land surface conditions through rainfall infiltration coefficients, while subsurface structures were parameterized using equivalent hydraulic conductivity ( K eq ) derived from effective medium theory. Validation results show that the model achieved a maximum error of only 1.7%, demonstrating reliable performance in predicting groundwater seepage. There is 23.23% area with GWL declining more than 0.4 m in the actual scenario with 93% impervious surface hardening comparing without surface hardening. Prediction scenarios with varying reduction rates of impervious surface compared with the actual scenario ( R a ) were conducted to investigate the impact of surface hardening on GWL. The results indicate average GWL of the study area presents exponential decay with the impervious surface ratio. Further, the variations in GWL of Aq0 were investigated by reducing hardened surfaces in different locations with the same R a . As the proportion of underground structures in the reduced impervious surface increases, the area with the same increment of GWL decreases. Prioritizing low impact development in areas with lower subsurface structure density can significantly enhance the efficiency of groundwater recharge by rainfall infiltration.

papers.title: Closed-Form Solutions for Temperature-Dependent Suction Stress under Transient Infiltration in Unsaturated Soil: An Application for Stability Analysis of Strip Plate Anchors
papers.summary: Abstract The soil layer up to a certain depth below the ground surface exists in an unsaturated state, where factors such as precipitation, evaporation, and prolonged subsurface heat waves control the state and material properties of soil. The suction stress that contributes to the resistance of the soil mass governs the stability of geostructures and depends on the thermal and hydraulic interactions in unsaturated soil. No solutions are available to determine the suction stress in soils subjected to transient flow conditions at elevated temperatures. This study develops closed-form expressions for temperature-dependent suction stress under transient flow conditions using the one-dimensional transient flow equation and a temperature-dependent soil–water retention curve. The developed equation was implemented within the framework of stress-based finite-element limit analysis to evaluate the stability of strip plate anchors in terms of their uplift capacity embedded in unsaturated sand, silt, and clay under transient flow conditions and varying temperatures. The critical role of thermal and hydraulic interactions in different types of unsaturated soils (clay, silt, and sand), specifically regarding matric suction, effective degree of saturation, and suction stress over time, has been discussed in detail. Additionally, a comprehensive parametric study has been conducted to evaluate the effects of transient flow and elevated temperature on the uplift capacity of shallow strip plate anchors. The results indicate that the behavior of plate anchors in unsaturated sand and silt is distinctly different from that in clay.

papers.title: Vertical Acceleration Effect on Slope Stability: A Simplified Coupled Insight
papers.summary: Abstract The paper focuses on the effect of the vertical ground acceleration component on slope stability. The proposed stability method is based on Newmark’s sliding block concept, which provides an intuitive indicator of slope stability. Contrary to the original Newmark method, both components of excitations, tangent and normal to the slip plane, are considered in force equilibrium. In the paper, the extended Newmark method is coupled with dynamic response obtained using the FEM and a direct time-integration scheme. Coupling the simple stability approach with the stress distribution history eliminates uncertainty in determining the intensity of the dynamic load acting on the sliding block. In the coupled method, the equilibrium of the sliding and resisting forces is considered along the discretized slip plane. When the limit equilibrium is reached, the relative movement of the block begins, and the permanent displacement of a sliding mass is accumulated. The influence of excitation components on permanent displacement is examined using a uniform steep slope as an example. The presented results indicate that shallow deformation mechanisms are more strongly affected by inertial forces than deeper ones. In the analyzed cases, the peak average acceleration for the shallow mechanism was between 1.2 and 3.0 times that for the deep mechanism. Furthermore, the effect of vertical acceleration on permanent displacements is notably more significant in shallow failure modes. It is shown that the permanent displacement obtained by the original Newmark’s method can be 74.3% lower than that obtained by the extended Newmark’s method. The impact of vertical acceleration itself can reach 24.6%.

papers.title: Rapid Assessment of Seismic Slope Stability Considering the Increase of Excess Pore-Water Pressure
papers.summary: Abstract For soil slopes, excess pore-water pressure (EPWP) buildup in soil elements is a major cause of slope failure during seismic loading. In this study, an EPWP coefficient was proposed and integrated into the simplified Bishop method to rapidly assess the influence of EPWP buildup on seismic slope stability and to calculate the slope factor of safety. To determine the value of the EPWP coefficient, numerical simulations of soil slopes with different inclinations were performed. During seismic loading, the decrease in the factor of safety for the slope can be clearly observed with the increase in EPWP. It was found that the value of the EPWP coefficient was negatively correlated with the slope angle. A linear function was employed to fit the correlation between the EPWP coefficient and the slope angle. It enables easy prediction of the EPWP coefficient based on the slope geometry and further facilitates seismic slope stability analysis that considers the EPWP buildup.

papers.title: Waste Dump Slope Stability and Toe Berm Stabilization Under Moisture-Induced Strength Degradation of a Thick Soft Loess Foundation
papers.summary: A waste dump at a copper–molybdenum mine in Chifeng, Inner Mongolia, China, was investigated. Direct shear tests, three-dimensional finite element analysis, and field monitoring were used to investigate the effects of moisture-induced strength degradation of the loess foundation on slope stability and the effectiveness of toe berms. As water content increased from 10% to 18%, the cohesion and internal friction angle of the loess decreased by 74.1% and 15.0%, respectively. As the shear strength of the foundation decreased, deformation became increasingly concentrated near the slope toe. A continuous shear strain band developed from the toe into the loess foundation, while the factor of safety (FoS) decreased from 1.93 to 1.08. Field monitoring showed that cumulative horizontal displacement increased from the crest toward the toe, a spatial pattern qualitatively consistent with the numerical results. With the 20 and 40 m toe berms, FoS increased to 1.25 and 1.35, respectively. With the 40 m berm, the maximum absolute vertical displacement in the model and maximum shear strain decreased by 81.0% and 74.1%, respectively, compared with the case without a berm. These results help characterize the stability of waste dumps with similar thick soft loess foundations and the effects of toe berms.

papers.title: Landslide Dams Triggered by Extreme Rainfall Events: A Tairāwhiti Gisborne Case Study
papers.summary: Landslide dams, formed when landslide debris blocks a river, occur across Aotearoa New Zealand. These events pose serious hazards to downstream communities and infrastructure, as sudden breaches can result in unexpected flooding and debris flows. They are also important components of complex cascading slope-river systems. Despite their contribution to sediment cascades and potential flood hazard, they remain under-researched. Understanding the interactions between hydrological, geological, and climatic factors governing landslide dam evolution is crucial for hazard management planning. The Tairāwhiti Gisborne region on the East Coast of Aotearoa New Zealand is prone to landslides and subsequent dams, due to its steep slopes, susceptible lithology, and exposure to tropical storms from the east. Despite this vulnerability, very little is known about the material properties and behaviour of landslide dams in this area. The primary aim of this thesis was to investigate the geomorphic and geotechnical aspects of dams in the Tairāwhiti Gisborne region, to understand their formation and breach processes. Two large landslide dams were chosen as case studies, the 1,485,500 m3 Waiorongomai Landslide Dam which formed in the north of the region in early January 2023, and the 98,500 m3 Tiniroto Landslide Dam which formed in the south of the region on the 3rd of October 2023. Three elements of analyses were used to investigate these landslide dams. First, historic landslides were mapped in the two catchments, to investigate the rate of landslide-river connectivity and landslide dam frequency. Each landslide source and deposit were mapped as polygons, using aerial imagery between 1988 and 2023. Second, the short-term evolution of the Waiorongomai and Tiniroto landslide dams was documented through a series of engineering geomorphic maps, using LiDAR and aerial imagery in ArcGIS Pro. Finally, the grain size distribution, liquid and plastic limits, and slake durability were analysed

papers.title: Developing Mitigation Measures against Rainfall-induced Shallow Landslides using Plant Root Systems
papers.summary: Rainfall-induced shallow landslides are rapid slope failures within shallow soil layers, generally less than 2 m thick, that are triggered by intense or prolonged rainfall on steep soilmantled slopes.NASA's Global Landslide Catalog recorded 11,033 reported rainfall-triggered landslides during 2007-2019, and an overlay with the FAO land-cover map indicated that up to 80% occurred in vegetated land-cover types.These observations show that vegetation does not uniformly prevent landslides.Its stabilizing effect has conventionally been represented mainly as additional root cohesion, although rainfall-induced instability is controlled by interactions among precipitation, hydrological responses, root-system architecture, soil depth, and the potential failure zone.Roots can increase mechanical resistance while also modifying infiltration, preferential flow, runoff, soil-water redistribution, saturation, and pore-waterpressure development.Consequently, the same root system can reinforce shallow soil but promote hydrological weakening where water is transferred beneath the principal rooting zone.

papers.title: Landslide susceptibility mapping using a physically-based model: the May 2023 Emilia-Romagna meteorological event
papers.source: AMS Laurea Institutional Research Repository (University of Bologna)
papers.summary: Rainfall-induced shallow landslides are an increasingly frequent hazard, with a direct impact on the land and on the people who live on it. Physically-based models assess their susceptibility by coupling a mechanical stability analysis with a hydrological description of the slope. The difficulty lies in the choice of the input parameters. The geotechnical and hydrological properties these models require cannot be measured at catchment scale: they have to be assumed within plausible intervals and calibrated on the observed landslides. Two major rainfall events struck the Emilia-Romagna region of Italy in May 2023. They triggered thousands of shallow landslides in the Apennine sector, mostly debris slides and debris flows, on slopes where no instability had been recorded before. This thesis applies the Fast Shallow Landslide Assessment Model (FSLAM) to the municipal territory of Casola Valsenio (84 km², 100 to 960 m a.s.l.), calibrating and evaluating it on the inventory compiled immediately afterwards. The purpose is not the best performance the model can give, but a measure of what each modelling choice is worth. Six configurations were compared on a common basis, fixed in advance: the validation dataset, the search space of the parameters and the selection rule. They differ in the calibration strategy and in the structure of the model. Across the six, accuracy ranges from 0.653 to 0.665 and the area under the ROC curve from 0.703 to 0.740, while the parameter sets that produce them differ by orders of magnitude. What the choices do change is the operating point of the model, the plausibility of the calibrated parameters and the consistency of the state of the slopes before the event. Accuracy alone therefore cannot select the parameters. Physical plausibility has to be set as a criterion before the calibration, not read off the results afterwards. What limits the model here is not its formulation, but the spatial information it can draw on.

This thesis provides an evaluation of the regional LEWS in Catalonia, Spain, assessing its real-time operational performance and sensitivity across operational factors (2024–2025) and its forecast reliability across 24 h and 48 h predictive lead times (2024–2026). The system inputs include precipitation datasets, Quantitative Precipitation Estimates (QPE) and Quantitative Precipitation Forecasts (QPF), alongside a regional static susceptibility map and an official reported landslide inventory The evaluation framework applies an adapted Event-Duration Matrix (EDuMaP) methodology combined with spatial-fuzzy verification across slope units, municipalities, and counties. Real-time evaluations against reported landslide inventories showed that applying quality-control data filtering and a 48 h fuzzy verification window significantly improved system Hit Rates, confirming that inventory timing uncertainties often mask successful alerts. Factor sensitivity and multi-factor clustering revealed that during that while the real-time forecasting the system captures medium-to-large shallow slides and debris flows during intense convective storms (𝐼𝑒𝑞 higher than 50 mm/h, detecting 80–85% of events), structural blind spots exist.
